title: 2  How to think under uncertainty
text:
2.7 Many heads: prediction markets
Everything so far has concerned a single mind: the superforecaster forming and revising her own probabilities, and the individual deciding whether to buy a ticket or accept an invitation to screen. A prediction market scales the same reasoning to many minds at once and reads the result off a price.
A prediction market trades contracts that pay a fixed sum — say €1 — if a specified event occurs and nothing if it does not. A contract on “candidate X wins the election” trading at €0.60 implies that the market values a euro paid only if X wins at 60 cents, which is to say it puts the probability of X winning at about 0.60. The price is a probability, and so, as the section on probability as risk noted, a risk — but one set by the trades of many people rather than asserted by one. A trader who judges the true probability higher than the price buys the contract in the expectation of profit; one who judges it lower sells; their trading pushes the price until it reflects the balance of the information the traders hold. Information scattered across many people, each holding a fragment, is aggregated into one continuously updated number. This is the wisdom of crowds — the observation that an aggregate of many independent judgements is often more accurate than any single judgement41 — with two additions: a price mechanism to combine the views, and money at stake to reward being right.
The money is what separates a market from a poll. A pundit pays no price for a confident forecast that proves wrong; a trader loses the stake, so posturing and wishful thinking are penalised and genuine information is rewarded. The market also performs the small-step updating described earlier, but collectively and in public: each trade is an incremental revision, and the price tracks events as they unfold. The forecasts are often accurate. The Iowa Electronic Markets, a small real-money market run for research since 1988, have predicted US presidential vote shares closer to the eventual result than the opinion polls a majority of the time, with their advantage greatest well before election day.42 In 2008 a group of prominent economists, several of them Nobel laureates, argued that markets aggregate dispersed information efficiently enough to deserve a wider role in business and government forecasting.43 A prediction market is, in this sense, institutionalised Bayesian aggregation: it turns many people’s background knowledge and evidence into a price that is a risk, with the profit motive standing in for the lone forecaster’s calibration.
Markets are not infallible, and their limits are instructive. The price equals the average probability only approximately: when traders are risk-averse and disagree, it is a wealth- and risk-weighted aggregate, and documented distortions such as the favourite–longshot bias — long shots over-priced, favourites under-priced — can skew it.44 A thin market, with few traders and little money, produces noisy prices that are easier to manipulate. And some markets should not exist at all: in 2003 the United States Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency proposed a Policy Analysis Market in contracts on political and military events in the Middle East, including acts of terrorism; once public, it was condemned in the Senate as a betting parlour on atrocities and cancelled within a day, and the official responsible resigned. The episode marks an ethical limit — some events should not be traded — alongside the legal and political obstacles such markets face more broadly.45 Used within those limits, a prediction market is among the most effective machines yet found for the aggregation that a superforecaster performs inside one well-trained head.






When the stakes are not money



The price in a money market is a money-weighted probability, and the distortions just noted follow from that: when traders are risk-averse and unequally wealthy, the price aggregates their beliefs in proportion to the money they stake, not the information they hold. This is the same gap that ran through the expected-value sections — money is a workable but imperfect proxy for the thing actually wanted, there a value, here an accurate probability.
Some platforms therefore drop the money. Metaculus, a forecasting platform running since 2015, asks users for explicit probabilities rather than trades and combines them into a community forecast — a recency-weighted median, with versions that weight contributors by their past accuracy. There is no cash; forecasters are scored by a strictly proper rule, for which the best strategy is to report one’s true belief, and are ranked on a track record built over many resolved questions.46 Play-money markets such as Manifold keep the trading mechanism but settle in points rather than currency. Each replaces the financial incentive with a reputational one.
The notable finding is that dropping the money costs little accuracy — and, against intuition, does not clearly raise it. In a head-to-head over an American-football season a play-money market forecast about as well as a real-money one, and across other questions the two stayed close, with real money tending to hold a slight edge where the odds were not common knowledge; no study finds play money the more accurate.47 One might expect the wealth-weighting of a money market, where deeper pockets lead to louder voices, to handicap it, but the distortion is apparently offset by what the stakes also buy: a sharper incentive to do the costly work of finding information, and to trade against a mispriced contract. Take the money away and the distortion and the incentive go together. Where non-monetary aggregation has clearly outperformed, the edge has come from the aggregation method rather than the absence of cash: in the tournaments behind this chapter’s superforecasters, prediction polls combined with performance weighting and recalibration beat trading markets, though those same markets still beat a naive average of the polls.48
The Good Judgment Project, the chapter’s opening, was itself non-monetary, ranking forecasters by Brier score rather than profit. The lesson rhymes with the one from expected value: what a market needs is not money as such, but an incentive aligned with being right and a sound way to combine many views. Money supplies both at once; where it brings distortions, or where the question is one no one should — or legally could — bet on, accuracy-scored aggregation can stand in for it.


Markets and superforecasters alike are devices for overcoming the flaws in ordinary individual judgement. Those flaws are systematic, they are well documented, and they are the subject of the rest of the chapter.

title: 2  How to think under uncertainty
section: 2.8 How thinking goes wrong: Tversky and Kahneman
text:
2.8 How thinking goes wrong: Tversky and Kahneman
The flaws are best seen against the standard set earlier — the habits of good reasoning in the chapter’s opening sections. Most people, most of the time, do not reason that way, and the departures are not random: they are systematic, shared across people, and predictable. The research programme that mapped them was begun by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in the 1970s, and it is convenient to set it against the two-system sketch Kahneman later drew.49 One mode of thought is fast, automatic, and effortless, and it answers a hard question by quietly substituting an easier one. Asked how probable is this? — a judgement that requires weighing the evidence against a base rate — it reaches instead for a question that can be settled without effort, such as how much does this resemble a typical case? or how readily does an example come to mind?, and reports the answer to that easy question as though it were the answer to the hard one. The swap goes unnoticed: the reasoner does not register that the question has changed. The three heuristics below are three versions of this same move. The other mode is slow, effortful, and deliberate, able to apply the rules of probability but lazy, and easily satisfied by the first answer the fast mode offers. The fast mode runs on heuristics — mental shortcuts that are economical and usually serviceable, but that produce characteristic errors. Tversky and Kahneman identified three.50
Representativeness judges how probable something is by how closely it resembles a stereotype, and in doing so discards information a calibrated reasoner would keep. Three of its errors recur in science.
The first is base-rate neglect, the discarding of the prior. In a much-used problem, a town’s taxis are 85% green and 15% blue; a witness who correctly identifies a cab’s colour 80% of the time reports that a cab in a night-time accident was blue. Combining the witness’s reliability with the base rate gives a probability of about 0.41 that the cab was blue; most people answer close to 0.80 — the witness’s reliability alone — neglecting the 15% base rate entirely. The failure is at the first of the four habits: the prior is thrown away.
The second is insensitivity to sample size, the neglect of how much small samples vary. A larger and a smaller hospital each record the proportion of male births every day; over a year, which more often records days on which more than 60% of births are boys? The smaller, because small samples fluctuate more widely around the true rate — yet most people judge the two equally likely. The error misreads the weight of a piece of evidence, treating a small and noisy sample as though it carried the information of a large one.
The third is the conjunction fallacy. Given a description of a woman built to fit the stereotype of a feminist, people judge “she is a bank teller and a feminist” more probable than “she is a bank teller” — though a conjunction can never be more probable than one of its parts.51 Representativeness here overrides a rule of probability so basic that stating it feels pedantic.
Availability judges the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, and emotionally charged events are recalled more readily and so are overweighted: people overestimate deaths from plane crashes and murders, which are reported and dramatic, and underestimate deaths from commoner but mundane causes such as falls. The error substitutes retrievability for diagnosticity — it lets the ease of recalling an example stand in for the weight of evidence the example carries.
Anchoring and adjustment lets an initial number, even a plainly irrelevant one, pull an estimate towards it, with the subsequent adjustment typically too small. People who watch a wheel of fortune stop on an arbitrary number, and are then asked to estimate an unrelated quantity, give answers biased towards that number. Anchoring corrupts the updating step: belief is dragged from an arbitrary starting point and moves too little to escape it.
A fourth pattern is not a heuristic but a consequence of how options are described. Framing effects arise when the same information, presented differently, reverses a choice.52 The case closest to this book is medical: when patients, students, and physicians chose between surgery and radiotherapy for lung cancer, surgery was far more attractive when its outcome was framed as “90% survive” than as “10% die”, though the two statements carry identical information.53 This is the same phenomenon as the relative-versus-absolute and survival-versus-mortality framings of the screening section, and it offends a principle from the section on probability as risk: a probability is the same probability however it is dressed.
Last, overconfidence: stated certainty routinely outruns accuracy. Asked for a range they are 90% sure contains some true value, people give ranges that contain it far less often than nine times in ten; asked how sure they are, they claim more than the record warrants.54 This is miscalibration, the opposite of the discipline that defines the superforecaster, and it is why calibration has to be learned and tracked rather than assumed.
These errors are usually presented, as they have been here, as a list of named biases. The next section asks whether a list is the right way to organise them.

title: 2  How to think under uncertainty
section: 2.9 A critical look at a nomenclature of irrationality
text:
2.9 A critical look at a nomenclature of irrationality
The biases of the previous section are usually met as a list — in textbooks, in the online “bias” catalogues, and in §2.8 above. A list invites the reader to memorise names; it does not show how the errors are related, and relatedness is what a scientist needs, because one underlying failure can appear under several names. It is worth saying first why the catalogue matters at all. These errors are not the preserve of the innumerate: they persist among people who have mastered probability and statistics, who reproduce them whenever they reason quickly rather than deliberately. Rational thinking is a competence partly separate from intelligence (the rationality-quotient callout earlier in the chapter gives the evidence), which is why it must be taught and why expertise does not confer exemption.55






Glossary of the named biases



The biases named in this chapter, defined for reference. The list is alphabetical — a place to look a term up; the organisation that makes the terms useful is supplied by the section, not by the list.

Ambiguity effect. Preferring a risk whose probability is known to one whose probability is unknown, even when the two offer the same prospects — an error on the value side, not in the belief.
Anchoring (and adjustment). Letting an initial number, even an irrelevant one, pull an estimate towards it, then adjusting too little to break free.
Availability. Judging how probable an event is by how easily examples come to mind, so that vivid, recent, or emotionally charged cases are overweighted.
Base-rate neglect. Estimating a probability from the specific evidence while ignoring how common the outcome is to begin with — discarding the prior.
Confirmation bias. Giving more weight to evidence that agrees with a held belief than to evidence that tells against it.
Conjunction fallacy. Judging a combination of two conditions more probable than one of them alone, which cannot be.
Conservatism (under-reaction). Revising a belief by too little when new evidence arrives.
Expected-value / expected-utility confusion. Treating money, or another raw outcome, as the quantity to maximise when what matters is its utility to the decision-maker.
Framing. Being moved by how identical information is described — “90% survive” versus “10% die”, or a gain versus an equivalent loss.
Gambler’s fallacy. Expecting independent chance outcomes to even out in the short run, so that a run of one result makes the other seem due.
Illusion of certainty (overconfidence). Stating more confidence than accuracy warrants; ranges meant to be 90% sure of containing a value contain it far less often.
Insensitivity to sample size. Treating a result from a small sample as if it were as reliable as one from a large sample, ignoring that small samples vary more.
Magical and conspiratorial thinking. Reading intention or hidden structure into events produced by chance.
Over-reaction (volatility). Revising a belief by too much with each new datum, lurching from one position to the next.
Reference-class error. Setting a prior from a comparison group that is too narrow, or chosen to flatter a desired conclusion.
Regression to the mean. The tendency of an extreme measurement to be followed by a less extreme one, often mistaken for a real effect.
Representativeness. Judging how probable something is by how closely it resembles a stereotype or typical case, while discarding other relevant information.



The obvious step beyond a flat list is to group the biases by theme. One such grouping sorts them under three headings: belief-updating errors, the neglect of randomness, and the over-imposition of causal structure. It is the kind of scheme that suggests itself readily, and worth dissecting for that reason, because the organising principle of a catalogue determines what it can teach.
Part of the scheme is sound. Filing the updating errors as two opposed kinds — underweighting new data (clinging to a first impression) and overweighting it (lurching with each new datum) — correctly identifies them as the two directions of a single fault, the misjudged size of an update. The difficulty is with almost everything filed around that core.

It is not mutually exclusive: the same error appears in several places under different names. “Anchoring”, filed as the intake of irrelevant information, and “availability”, filed as the undervaluing of relevant information, are mirror images of one fault — assigning a datum the wrong evidential weight. “Overweighting emotionally charged information” is availability again, listed a second time under a different heading. Insensitivity to sample size is filed both under overweighting new data and under the neglect of randomness.
It is not exhaustive in any principled way: framing and overconfidence are appended to the causal-structure heading, with which they have nothing to do, because there is nowhere else to put them.
It files some errors in the wrong place entirely: the ambiguity effect — a preference for risks whose probabilities are known over risks whose probabilities are not — is listed as a belief-updating error, but it is not an error of belief at all. It is a feature of how options are valued, and belongs with decision-making.
It mixes two organising principles: the first heading sorts by the stage of belief updating, the other two by the type of metaphysical mistake. A catalogue cannot be read consistently if its branches answer different questions.

The root trouble is that the headings name the surface appearance of an error rather than the mechanism that produced it. The chapter has, by this point, built the mechanism: a reasoner sets a prior, weighs evidence, updates, checks calibration, and — when the belief is turned into a choice — attaches values. A more useful catalogue sorts each documented failure by the stage that broke.

Errors of the prior — reasoning from the wrong background knowledge, or from none: base-rate neglect, and the choice of a too-narrow or self-serving reference class.
Errors in the weight of evidence — giving a datum the wrong diagnostic weight: availability (over-weighting the vivid and the easily recalled), anchoring (over-weighting an irrelevant number), confirmation bias (over-weighting agreeable data), and insensitivity to sample size (treating weak evidence as strong).
Errors in the updating step — moving belief by the wrong amount: under-reaction and conservatism on one side, over-reaction and volatility on the other. This is the sound core of the thematic scheme, kept intact.
Errors of calibration — confidence not matched to accuracy: overconfidence and the illusion of certainty.
Misreadings of randomness — reading structure into noise, or noise into structure: the gambler’s fallacy, regression to the mean mistaken for an effect, conspiracy and magical thinking, and the conjunction fallacy. Formally these are one error — using the wrong likelihood, misjudging how probable the data are under chance — but they form a recognisable family worth naming together.
Errors on the value side — failures that arise only when a belief is turned into a decision, not in the belief itself: the ambiguity effect, the gain-versus-loss framing of outcomes, and the confusion of expected value with expected utility.

Cutting across all six is framing, or more generally the representation of the problem: the same facts described differently change the answer, so a framing effect can corrupt the input to any stage. It is not a seventh category but a property of the channel through which information reaches every other one.
No taxonomy of this kind is perfectly exclusive — confirmation bias, for instance, breaks both the weight-of-evidence stage and the updating stage at once. But sorting by mechanism has a payoff a list of names cannot offer: it tells the scientist what to check. An error in the prior is repaired by finding the right reference class; an error of calibration, by keeping score; a misreading of randomness, by asking what a chance process alone would produce. The name of a bias is a label; its location in the pipeline is a diagnosis.
A deeper objection questions whether these patterns deserve the name “errors” at all — the reason “right” and “wrong” have carried quotation marks since the first page of the chapter. A heuristic that violates a rule of probability in a textbook problem may be the better policy in the environment it was acquired for, where information is scarce, costly, and quickly out of date. Simple rules that deliberately ignore information show “less-is-more” effects: a rule that bases a judgement on a single good cue can match or beat multiple regression when forecasts are tested out of sample, because it has less opportunity to overfit the noise in past data.56 A mind that economises on information can handle an uncertain world more robustly than one that tries to weigh everything.57 “Right” and “wrong” thinking are therefore relative to the task and its environment. The normative pipeline of this chapter is the correct standard when the question is a well-posed probability problem with the relevant information to hand — the situation of most scientific inference, and the reason the rest of the book adopts it — but it is not the only standard for a mind operating under real constraints. The scientist’s task is to recognise which of the two regimes she is in, and to reserve the machinery of formal probability for the problems that reward it.
That machinery is what the next part of the book builds. The habits sketched here informally — prior, evidence, updating, calibration — are, formally, the rules of probability, and Part II derives them twice over: as the unique logic of consistent belief, and as the mathematics of counting. The remainder of the book is then concerned with the harder question these tools leave open: not how to update belief on evidence, but how to read a causal claim out of it.

title: 2  How to think under uncertainty
text:
2.10 Key points

Good reasoning under uncertainty is a learnable disposition, not a calculation. The superforecaster exemplifies it; it persists despite, not because of, raw intelligence, and must be practised.
That disposition is Bayesian inference without the arithmetic: start from base rates (the prior), weigh each datum by how diagnostic it is (the weight of evidence), update in small steps, and keep stated probabilities calibrated, aggregating diverse views where possible.
A probability is a risk. The same risk stated in relative and in absolute terms invites opposite intuitions; a careful reasoner reads through to the absolute numbers.
Expected value, \(\sum_i p_i v_i\), is the one tool for turning probabilities into decisions — but the quantity to maximise is expected utility, not money (the lottery), and for some decisions the outcomes share no objective scale, so the utilities are personal and no single public expected value can settle the choice (screening).
Prediction markets aggregate dispersed information into a price that is a probability; they are powerful within limits set by thin trading, known pricing biases, and ethics.
The documented biases are systematic departures from the four habits. They are most usefully organised not as a flat list but by the stage of reasoning that fails — prior, weight of evidence, updating, calibration, or the value side — with framing cutting across all of them.
“Right” and “wrong” are relative to the task. The formal pipeline is the right standard for well-posed scientific inference; simple heuristics can be the better policy under real constraints.

title: 2  How to think under uncertainty
text:
2.11 Exercises

The cab problem by Bayes. A town’s cabs are 85% green and 15% blue; a witness who is correct 80% of the time reports a blue cab. Confirm by hand, or in R, that the probability the cab was blue is about 0.41. Then recompute it with the base rate set to 50% green / 50% blue, and explain in one sentence what the base rate contributes.
When is the lottery worth it? Using the EuroJackpot figures in the lottery section (ticket €2, jackpot odds 1 in 139,838,160), find the jackpot at which the jackpot’s contribution alone equals the ticket price. Then add a hypothetical second tier — €1,000 at odds of 1 in 5,000 — and recompute the expected value. Does it change the conclusion?
Benefit against harm. From the UK Panel’s figures (43 deaths prevented and 129 cancers overdiagnosed per 10,000 women invited over 20 years), compute the number of women who must be invited to prevent one death, and the ratio of overdiagnoses to deaths prevented. Compare with the Cochrane review’s roughly 1-to-10 ratio and give two reasons the two reviews differ.
Keep score. Over one week, write down ten predictions about your own life or the news as probabilities (for example, “70% it rains tomorrow”). After the events resolve, compute your Brier score and group the forecasts by stated confidence. Were the events you called “90%” right about nine times in ten?
Place the bias. Take three biases not discussed in the chapter — say hindsight bias, the sunk-cost fallacy, and the planning fallacy — and assign each to a stage of the pipeline scheme in the critical-look section. For any that break more than one stage, say which and why.
Conceptual: the anecdote. Using the idea of the weight of evidence, explain why a single vivid anecdote should move a calibrated reasoner less than it moves most people, and connect your answer to the availability heuristic.

crumbs: 2  How to think under uncertainty

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
3.1 Two assumptions generate the whole calculus
The construction device, which we will reuse in Chapter 7, is due to Jaynes.1 Imagine a robot: an idealised reasoner that we design ourselves, free of the biases catalogued in the previous chapter. The robot receives propositions — statements that are either true or false, such as “the patient was treated” or “the patient had a stroke within five years” — and must compute judgements about compound statements built from them. We give the robot two design specifications:
Everything in this chapter follows from these two specifications. Both are substantive assumptions, not platitudes. Bivalence fails for propositions whose truth is not yet settled — the historical aside at the end of this chapter — and it is the assumption that Part II of this book weakens. Truth-functionality fails for causal statements, as discussed below under the conditional, and repairing that failure requires the separate machinery of Part III. Each limit of the calculus can thus be traced to the assumption that produces it.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
Bivalence. Every proposition carries one of two values, TRUE or FALSE. There is no third value, and the robot is never permitted to answer “it depends” or “unknown”.
Truth-functionality. The truth value of a compound proposition is fully determined by the truth values of its parts. To evaluate “A AND B” the robot consults the value of A and the value of B, and nothing else — not their subject matter, not their history, not any causal relation between them.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
section: 3.2 The connectives are counted, not chosen
text:
3.2 The connectives are counted, not chosen
A truth table lists every possible assignment of truth values to the elementary propositions. With two propositions A and B there are four rows: both true, only A true, only B true, neither true. Each row is one possible state of the world, as far as A and B are concerned, and together the rows are a complete case analysis: whatever the world is like, it is described by one of the rows.
By truth-functionality, a connective is a rule that fills in one output column of such a table. The familiar connectives are:


Show code
tf <- function(x) ifelse(x, "T", "F")
a <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
b <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
tibble(A = tf(a), B = tf(b),
       `NOT A` = tf(!a),
       `A AND B` = tf(a & b),
       `A OR B` = tf(a | b),
       `A -> B` = tf(!a | b),
       `A IFF B` = tf(a == b)) %>%
  kable()

NOT A is true when A is false. A AND B is true only in the row where both parts are true. A OR B is false only in the row where both parts are false (this is the inclusive “or”: one or the other or both). The conditional A -> B and the biconditional A IFF B are discussed in their own section below. In the logical literature these connectives are written \(\lnot A\), \(A \land B\), \(A \lor B\), \(A \to B\) and \(A \leftrightarrow B\); we keep the word forms, which match the R output.
The two design specifications do more than license these particular connectives: they fix the complete inventory. A connective with two inputs must assign T or F to each of the four rows, so there are \(2^4 = 16\) possible binary connectives — no fewer, no more, and none outside the following table. The same counting works at any arity: there are four unary connectives (of which only negation deserves a name) and, in general, \(2^{2^n}\) connectives of \(n\) inputs. The systematic study of all truth functions goes back to Post.2

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
3.3 One connective is enough
Logical implication is a convenience rule rather than a fundamental rule of logic. The whole of propositional logic can be generated from several small sets of connectives: {AND, NOT}, {OR, NOT}, or even the single connective NAND — NOT(A AND B) — or the single connective NOR.3 This is why one can build computers that use a single type of logic gate. A NAND gate’s output is up when at least one of the inputs is down, and down when both inputs are up; by combining NAND gates one can create any logic function. The following table verifies the constructions of NOT, AND and OR from NAND alone — and since {AND, NOT} generate everything, so does NAND:


Show code
nand <- function(x, y) !(x & y)
tibble(A = tf(a), B = tf(b),
       `NOT A` = tf(!a),
       `NAND(A, A)` = tf(nand(a, a)),
       `A AND B` = tf(a & b),
       `NAND(NAND(A,B), NAND(A,B))` = tf(nand(nand(a, b), nand(a, b))),
       `A OR B` = tf(a | b),
       `NAND(NAND(A,A), NAND(B,B))` = tf(nand(nand(a, a), nand(b, b)))) %>%
  kable()

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
section: 3.4 Entailment: truth preserved in every row
text:
3.4 Entailment: truth preserved in every row
The truth table also defines what a valid argument is. An argument from premises to a conclusion is valid — the premises entail the conclusion — when every row that makes all the premises true also makes the conclusion true. Because the rows are a complete case analysis, validity can be checked mechanically: write out the table, find the rows where the premises all hold, inspect the conclusion there. The Socrates argument in its propositional form is the pattern called modus ponens:


Show code
tibble(A = tf(a), B = tf(b),
       `premise 1: A -> B` = tf(!a | b),
       `premise 2: A` = tf(a),
       `all premises true` = tf((!a | b) & a),
       `conclusion: B` = tf(b)) %>%
  kable()

Only the first row makes both premises true, and in that row the conclusion is true; the argument is valid. Note what validity does and does not promise. It transmits truth: if the premises are true, the conclusion is true. If a premise is false, a valid argument promises nothing about the conclusion — the guarantee in the schema at the start of this chapter requires both the true premises and the correct algorithm.
A set of propositions is consistent when at least one row makes all of them true, and inconsistent when no row does. Inconsistency has a drastic consequence: by the definition just given, an inconsistent set entails every proposition whatsoever, because there is no row where all the premises hold and the conclusion fails. A single contradiction therefore does not produce one wrong conclusion; it removes the distinction between conclusions and non-conclusions.
Checking validity row by row and deriving conclusions step by step from rules (such as repeated modus ponens) are two different procedures, and it is a theorem, not an accident, that they agree: every argument derivable by the standard rules is valid in the tables, and every tabularly valid argument is derivable. This completeness result for propositional logic is also due to Post, in the same 1921 paper.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
section: 3.5 Assertion as a contract: the sure-loss argument
text:
3.5 Assertion as a contract: the sure-loss argument
The truth-table definition of consistency has an operational counterpart, which we set out here because the book reuses it under uncertainty (Chapter 7). Read an assertion as a contract: by asserting a proposition, you accept a penalty of one unit, payable if the proposition turns out false. Denying B — asserting NOT B — means you pay one unit if B turns out true.
Suppose you assert all three of: A -> B, A, and NOT B.


Show code
loss <- function(true) ifelse(true, 0, -1)
tibble(A = tf(a), B = tf(b),
       `assert A -> B` = loss(!a | b),
       `assert A` = loss(a),
       `assert NOT B` = loss(!b)) %>%
  mutate(`net payoff` = `assert A -> B` + `assert A` + `assert NOT B`) %>%
  kable()

In every row the net payoff is negative: you pay at least one unit no matter how the world turns out. The loss is guaranteed by the form of the commitments alone, before any facts are in. This is what inconsistency means under the contract reading: a set of assertions is inconsistent when its penalty table has no zero-loss row, and consistent when at least one row leaves you unharmed. Entailment can be restated the same way: A entails B when asserting A while denying B is a guaranteed loss.
In this chapter commitments come in only two strengths — full assertion or none. Chapter 7 allows graded commitments, bets at any odds between 0 and 1, and shows that the requirement of avoiding guaranteed loss then forces the sum and product rules of probability. That result is the Dutch book argument.4 The penalty table above is its limiting case under certainty, and the parallel is worth stating in one line: inconsistency is a sure loss under certainty; incoherence is a sure loss under uncertainty.
One caveat applies to the sure-loss argument here, to the Dutch book, and equally to the desiderata route of Chapter 7. The argument reasons by cases over the rows of a truth table, and reasoning by cases is itself classical logic; a derivation of logic that uses logic is not a creation from nothing. What such constructions deliver is a short, explicit list of assumptions from which the calculus follows — so that when a rule is questioned, the question can be redirected to the assumption that produces it. That is the sense of “from first principles” used throughout this book.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
section: 3.6 What the conditional is, and what it is not
text:
3.6 What the conditional is, and what it is not
The conditional A -> B is FALSE if and only if A is TRUE and B is FALSE; in all other cases it is TRUE. It rules out one row of the table — the row where A holds and B fails — and asserts nothing more. In particular, A -> B does not say that B is deducible from A, that A is evidence for B, or that A brings B about. When B is true, A -> B is true whatever A is about; when A is false, A -> B is true whatever B is about. “If the Moon is made of cheese, then Tartu is in Estonia” is a true proposition, and in formal logic every true statement implies every other true statement. These so-called paradoxes of material implication are not defects of the calculus. They follow from truth-functionality: an “if” that may consult only two truth values has f11 in the table of sixteen as its only reasonable candidate, and f11 is what the candidate can do.
The everyday “if” is a different object, because it routinely carries causal content. Consider: “if the patient had not been treated, she would have had a stroke”. This is a counterfactual conditional. For a treated patient the antecedent is false, so the material reading makes the sentence automatically true — and it makes the opposite sentence, “if the patient had not been treated, she would not have had a stroke”, automatically true as well. Both cannot be informative, yet for a clinician one of them states the effect of the treatment and the other denies it. The truth of a counterfactual depends on what would have happened in an unrealised case, and that is not a function of the actual truth values of its parts. The counterfactual “if” violates truth-functionality, and no reassignment of rows can repair it, because the defect is in the inputs, not the output column. The machinery for such sentences — potential outcomes — is built in Part III (Chapter 10), after the ground is prepared in Chapter 4.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
3.7 Three things to remember

The concept of causality is not encoded in logic. Logic is about co-occurrence of A and B; it cannot even express the thought that A might be a cause of B. As the previous section shows, this is not an omission that a better connective could fix: causal conditionals violate truth-functionality itself. The mathematical description of causal relations is its own subject, independent of classical logic, probability theory and statistical inference (Chapter 4 and Part III).
Propositional logic is monotonic, meaning that once a conclusion is achieved, it cannot in principle be changed. Getting new data after forming one’s conclusions makes no difference — once you have a conclusion, this conclusion stands forever.
Logic is deductive, like mathematics — it provides risk-free arguments, with the downside that technically no new information can be brought into being by a logical argument. Logic is an axiomatic system, like geometry. From axioms one can deduce theorems, a.k.a. rules for doing stuff, but these rules are already embedded in the axioms.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
section: 3.8 The strong syllogisms and the weak ones
text:
3.8 The strong syllogisms and the weak ones
Classical logic licenses two inference patterns built on the conditional, which Jaynes calls the strong syllogisms:

Modus ponens. A -> B; A is true; therefore B is true.
Modus tollens. A -> B; B is false; therefore A is false.

Both are valid in the truth-table sense, as checked above. But everyday and scientific reasoning constantly uses two further patterns, which Pólya called the weak syllogisms:5

A -> B; B is true; therefore A becomes more plausible.
A -> B; A is false; therefore B becomes less plausible.

A clinical example: suppose that if the patient has the disease, the antigen test is positive. The test comes back positive. The patient’s having the disease has not been proved — other conditions can also produce a positive test — but the result is evidence that bears on the diagnosis. As a classical inference this is the fallacy of affirming the consequent; as a description of how evidence accumulates, it is the daily operation of diagnosis, and of science generally.
Classical logic is not wrong about the weak syllogisms; it is silent about them. The conclusion “more plausible” is not TRUE or FALSE, so a bivalent calculus has no place to put it. This silence is the design specification for Part II: we need a calculus that reproduces the strong syllogisms as limiting cases and gives numerical content to the weak ones — by how much does a positive test raise the plausibility of disease? Chapters 5 and 7 construct that calculus by two independent routes, and Chapter 8 supplies the number (the weight of evidence).

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
3.9 An historical aside: three-valued logic
In 1465 Peter de Rivo of the University of Louvain was asked by a student a thorny question: after Christ had told St Peter “Thou wilt deny me thrice”, could St Peter, in principle, have refrained from denying Christ? If the answer had been “No”, then de Rivo would have committed the heresy of determinism (without free will there is little point in the Christian doctrine of salvation). On the other hand, had the answer been “Yes”, that would have made Christ a liar, at least potentially so. In the event, the professor’s answer was that St Peter did have the power not to deny Christ, but that this would not have made Christ a liar, because Christ’s utterance to St Peter was neither true nor false: it had a neutral truth value, and the contradictory of a neutral statement is itself neutral. Accordingly, the claim that St Peter did not deny Christ would be heretical only if it were false (in the sense that St Peter actually denied Christ as predicted). For a prediction about tomorrow to be true today, it must be unpreventably so: “Either there is no present and actual truth in the articles of faith about the future, or what they say is something that even a divine power cannot prevent.” This three-valued logic was condemned by the Pope in 1474, and the idea did not re-emerge until the twentieth century.6
The twentieth-century return happened in two steps, and the second connects directly to this chapter’s contract reading of assertion. Łukasiewicz published the first formal three-valued logic in 1920, with the third value read as “possible” and motivated by the same problem of future contingents that had been argued at Louvain.7 Then consider a bet on B made conditional on A: the bet is won if A and B are both true, lost if A is true and B is false, and called off, with the stake returned, if A is false. The called-off bet is neither a win nor a loss — a third outcome, forced by the structure of the contract. De Finetti developed this three-outcome structure into a logic of conditional events,8 and the called-off bet reappears in Chapter 7 as the operational definition of conditional probability.
The proof that we can build a self-contained probabilistic logic, in which between TRUE and FALSE lie the real numbers between 0 and 1, and which is fully compatible with the traditional bivalent logic, had to wait until the middle of the twentieth century.9






Varieties of logic



Propositional logic is one member of a family of formal systems. The family is organised by a single question: which of this chapter’s assumptions does each system keep, and which does it relax?

Propositional logic keeps bivalence and truth-functionality. It is consistent, complete and decidable: a truth table settles any question in a finite number of steps.
Predicate logic adds quantifiers (“for all”, “there exists”), which the Socrates syllogism needs in its original form. It keeps bivalence and completeness but loses decidability: no mechanical procedure exists that delivers a verdict on every argument in a finite number of steps.
Modal logics add the operators “necessarily” and “possibly”, which are not truth-functional: the truth value of “possibly A” is not determined by the truth value of A. Systems with the same structure handle time (“eventually A”), obligation (“A is required”) and knowledge (“the agent knows A”).
Many-valued logics relax bivalence, admitting a third truth value (the historical aside above) or more. Fuzzy logic admits a continuum: “the patient is hypertensive” can hold to degree 0.7. The degree measures how far a vague predicate applies; it is not a probability, which is a graded belief about a proposition that is itself either true or false.
Intuitionistic logic reads “A is true” as “A has a proof” and therefore gives up the law of excluded middle: when neither a proof nor a refutation of A exists, A OR NOT A cannot be asserted. It is the working logic of constructive mathematics.
Non-monotonic logics relax monotonicity (point 2 of “Three things to remember”): adding a premise can remove a conclusion. The standard example: birds fly, Tweety is a bird, so Tweety flies; on learning that Tweety is a penguin, the conclusion is withdrawn rather than contradicted. Classical logic cannot represent this pattern, yet it is the routine form of clinical judgement — a working diagnosis is held until further findings displace it. Formal versions (default logic, circumscription) were developed in artificial-intelligence research.10 They are qualitative: they state when a default conclusion is blocked, but not how much plausibility it loses.
Probability theory (Part II) is also a non-monotonic extension of classical logic, and a quantitative one: conditioning on new data moves the plausibility of a conclusion by a stated amount, and classical logic is recovered at the endpoints 0 and 1. Among the systems in this list, it is the one that satisfies the requirements collected at the end of this chapter, which is why this book adopts it.

The list shows that “logic” names a family of calculi, not a single doctrine. Each member is generated by assumptions, as in this chapter, and the choice among them is a question of which assumptions fit the reasoning task at hand.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
3.10 Logic and rational thought
This chapter opened with the claim that, under certainty, rational thinking is more or less logical thinking. With the calculus in hand, the claim can be assessed. Three observations separate logic from a complete account of rational thought, and a theorem of Gödel’s limits the deductive ideal on its own ground.
First, logic evaluates form, not content. A valid argument transmits the truth of the premises to the conclusion; it does not certify any premise. In the schema at the start of this chapter — true premises, correct algorithm, true conclusions — logic is responsible only for the algorithm. Whether the premises deserve belief is decided by measurement, study design and prior evidence, and none of that work is deductive.
Second, logic does not rank its conclusions. From any premise, infinitely many conclusions follow validly: A entails A OR B for every B whatsoever. Validity does not order this unbounded set by relevance or use, and derivation costs time. Which consequences are worth deriving depends on the reasoner’s goals, and the calculus does not represent goals. Rational thought is purposive; validity is indifferent to purpose.
Third, as a description of human reasoning, classical logic fails, and the failure is itself informative. In Wason’s selection task, the subject sees four cards showing A, K, 4 and 7, is told that every card has a letter on one side and a number on the other, and must select all the cards, and only the cards, that need to be turned over to test the rule “if a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side”.11 The rule can be refuted only by a card carrying a vowel and an odd number, and only the A card and the 7 card could turn out to be such a card; the K and the 4 cannot, since the rule says nothing about consonants and does not claim that an even number must have a vowel on its reverse. Only a small minority of subjects select A and 7; the most common choices are A alone, or A together with 4. Turning the 4 in the expectation that a vowel behind it would support the rule is the fallacy of affirming the consequent — a weak syllogism treated as if it were strong.
Oaksford and Chater showed that the same behaviour has a different status under a different standard.12 Read the task as inductive hypothesis testing: which cards are expected to yield the most information about whether the rule holds, in a world where vowels and even numbers are rare? Under that reading, the expected information gain of the four cards reproduces the order in which subjects actually choose them, and turning the 4 is close to optimal data selection. The same choice is a fallacy relative to the deductive standard and a near-optimal experiment relative to the informational one. A verdict of irrationality is therefore always relative to a normative standard, and the standard must be named. The biases catalogued in the previous chapter are read, in this book, against the standard built in Part II.

3.10.1 Gödel’s theorem: a limit from within
Propositional logic is consistent, complete and decidable. In the early twentieth century it was a live ambition — associated with Hilbert’s programme and with Russell and Whitehead’s Principia Mathematica — to extend this situation to the whole of mathematics: to fix a list of axioms and mechanical rules from which every mathematical truth follows, and to prove, by elementary means, that the system is consistent. Had the ambition succeeded, rationality in mathematics would have been reduced to computation: every question settled, in principle, by running the rules.
In 1931 Gödel proved that this cannot be done.13 Take any formal system that (i) is consistent, (ii) has a mechanically checkable list of axioms and rules, and (iii) is expressive enough to state elementary arithmetic — whole numbers with addition and multiplication. Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem states that such a system contains a sentence of arithmetic that the system can neither prove nor refute; on the standard reading of arithmetic, the sentence is true. The second incompleteness theorem identifies one such sentence: the statement that the system itself is consistent. A consistent system of this strength cannot prove its own consistency.
The argument can be given in outline. Gödel encoded sentences and proofs as numbers, so that “sentence number n is provable in this system” became itself a sentence of arithmetic, and he constructed a sentence G that, under the encoding, states “G is not provable in this system”. Suppose, for simplicity, that the system proves only true sentences. Then G cannot be provable, since a proof would make G false. So G is unprovable — which is what G states, so G is true: a true sentence the system cannot reach. Gödel’s published proof replaces the assumption that the system proves only truths with a weaker consistency assumption, at the price of a longer argument; the conclusion stands. An accessible book-length account is Nagel and Newman’s.14
Two boundaries on the result should be stated, because the theorem attracts overstatement. It applies to formal systems satisfying conditions (i)–(iii);15 it does not say that mathematical knowledge is unreliable, and the mathematics used in this book is unaffected by it in practice. Nor does it establish, by itself, any claim about human minds exceeding machines; such extensions require additional premises that are themselves disputed.
What the theorem does establish, for this chapter’s question, is narrow and definite: the identification of rationality with derivation inside one fixed formal system fails even in pure mathematics, the most favourable case available to it. With the axioms held certain, no such system reaches every truth of its own domain, and no such system certifies its own consistency; the reasons for trusting a formal system are always partly outside the system. This book proceeds accordingly: the present chapter derived logic from two assumptions, and Chapter 7 derives probability from a short list of desiderata, but in both cases the assumptions are defended by argument about the reasoning task, not proved within the calculus they generate.
None of this demotes logic. Deductive structure is what makes a scientific argument checkable, and the requirement that conclusions follow from stated premises is not negotiable. The conclusions of this section are specific: logic does not supply premises, does not rank conclusions, does not describe human reasoners. A normative account of scientific reasoning must therefore extend deduction rather than reproduce it, and the next section lists what the extension must do.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
3.12 Key points

Classical propositional logic follows from two design assumptions: bivalence (every proposition is TRUE or FALSE) and truth-functionality (the value of a compound depends only on the values of its parts).
The connectives are not a convention but a count: \(2^{2^n}\) connectives of \(n\) inputs, sixteen binary ones; small sets generate all of them, and NAND alone suffices.
Entailment is truth preservation in every row of the truth table; consistency is the existence of a row that makes all the propositions true. Both are checked by complete, mechanical case analysis.
Under the contract reading of assertion, inconsistency is a guaranteed loss; the same argument with graded commitments is the Dutch book (Chapter 7).
The material conditional rules out one row and asserts nothing more. The causal and counterfactual “if” of everyday language is not truth-functional; it requires the potential-outcomes machinery of Part III.
Logic is monotonic and deductive: conclusions do not change with new data, and no new information is created by a valid argument.
The strong syllogisms are valid; the weak syllogisms — where evidence accumulates — receive no truth value at all. Meeting that gap is the design specification for Part II.
“Logic” names a family of calculi distinguished by which classical assumption each relaxes: bivalence (many-valued and fuzzy logics), truth-functionality (modal logics), monotonicity (default logics and probability). Probability is the quantitative non-monotonic member, and the one this book adopts.
Logic is not a complete theory of rational thought: it does not certify premises, does not rank valid conclusions by relevance, and does not describe human performance (the selection task). By Gödel’s incompleteness theorems, no single consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic proves every truth of its domain, or its own consistency.

title: 3  Rational thinking under certainty
text:
3.13 Exercises

Count the connectives. Adapt the enumeration code to list all \(2^{2^1} = 4\) unary connectives (the truth table now has two rows). Name each one. How many ternary connectives are there, and why is enumerating them by hand no longer attractive?
NOR is also enough. Using only NOR — NOT(A OR B) — construct NOT A, A AND B, and A OR B, and verify your constructions by truth table, following the NAND chunk as a template.
AND and OR are not enough. Try to construct NOT A using only AND and OR (and the propositions themselves). Inspect the row in which every elementary proposition is TRUE: what value does any AND/OR compound take there, and what value must NOT A take? Conclude that {AND, OR} is not functionally complete.
A sure loss of your own. Build the penalty table for a reasoner who asserts A -> B, asserts NOT B, and also asserts A (violating modus tollens). Show that every row loses, and identify the row in which the reasoner loses twice.
Which “if” is truth-functional? Classify each sentence as capturable by the material conditional (f11) or not, with one sentence of justification each: (a) “If the p-value is below 0.05, the result is declared significant.” (b) “If the dose had been halved, the patient would have survived.” (c) “If the alarm sounds, there is a fire, because the alarm is triggered by smoke.”
Diagnosis as a weak syllogism. Take the premise “if the patient has the disease, the test is positive” to be true without exception (sensitivity 1). (a) The test is negative: which strong syllogism applies, and what does it license? (b) The test is positive: what does classical logic license, and what would you nevertheless conclude in practice? (c) Now suppose the premise holds for only 90% of diseased patients. Which of your answers survives, and in what form? (Chapter 8 returns to this calculation.)
Three-valued tables. Introduce a third value N (“neutral”) and order the values F < N < T. Let NOT swap T and F while fixing N; let AND return the minimum and OR the maximum of its inputs. Write out the three-valued tables for NOT, AND and OR, and show that A OR NOT A is no longer a tautology. Which row of your table is de Rivo’s defence of Christ’s prediction?
The selection task. Four cards show A, K, 4 and 7; every card has a letter on one side and a number on the other. The rule under test: “if a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side”. (a) State which cards must be turned over, and justify each choice — and each omission — using the strong syllogisms. (b) A subject turns the 4, expecting a vowel behind it to support the rule. Name the fallacy, and connect it to a weak syllogism. (c) Suppose vowels and even numbers are rare among cards in general. Argue informally that turning the 4 may then be expected to be more informative than turning the 7. (Chapter 8 supplies the machinery that makes “informative” precise.)

(ii) Mechanical checkability: an algorithm can decide, for any proposed proof, whether it follows the system’s axioms and rules; the axioms need not be finite in number, but they must be recognisable by machine. title: 4  Causal inference and Experiment
text:
4.1 Ancient theories of causality
Aristotle (384-322) offers 4 types of answers to the question “why?”
Aristotles causes and effects are usually not single events, like causation is commonly seen in modern philosophy, but more complex entities, like human beings or proportions or the skill of the sculptor. Effects can also be states, actions, substances, events. According to Aristotle, following the four causes will result in an natural science kind of explanation of things. So, we can think of these as explanatory tools, especially in the context of biology (but note that for Aristotle, physics explanations were not that different – to AI: I need an expansion here, with ref)
Stoics saw causation differently.1 They disregard material, formal and final causes, but espouse several different forms of efficient causes. They also offer a universal law of causation: A causes that B is F, where A and B are bodies, and F is an abstract non-bodily entity, a lekton. For example, A - scalpel, B- flesh, F - predicate “being cut”. A is the active element, while B is the passive element (also called matter).
The stoics accepted a strong causal determinism: (i) everything is caused by something, and (ii) every effect is fully determined by its cause(s). So, nothing happens without a cause and every cause is a necessitating cause (the effect cannot not happen, when there is cause). This unified series of causes and effects is the doctrine of fate. This, of course, brings on the question about free will. One way to get to free will is to posit with Epicurus (341-270) that the world is made of tiny atoms, which in addition to causal interactions have some amount of random unpredictable swerves. Or, alternatively, maybe the mind somehow has freedom of tought, although it is influenced by external causes (Chrysippus; b. 279 B.C.), or maybe there actually are no external antecedent causes for our will (Carneades; 214-129).

the material cause – this what things are made of.
the formal cause may be expressed in a definition. It is a form and a pattern of a thing. the proportion of the length of strings is the reason for different notes played on a lyre being an octave away.
the efficient cause – this the orgin of a change or state of rest. A person reaching a decision, a father who begets a child, a sculptor carving a statue, a doctor curing a patient.
the final cause is the end goal why something is done (doctor works to make the patient healthy, a lung works to oxygenate the body, etc.). For living things the formal and final causes coincide (the realization of a mature organism is the goal towards which the an organism strives).
