Only the share of red is known (30/90), so the bets on red and on black or yellow carry known odds, while the bets on black and on red or yellow carry unknown ones. Offered the choice, most people take the bet on red over the bet on black, and the bet on black or yellow over the bet on red or yellow — the known odds each time.
The two ideas now bite. By the representation theorem, anyone holding a single prior for the urn — treating the 60 unknown balls as, say, 30 black and 30 yellow — would score each bet by its chance of paying and rank the four once and for all. By the sure-thing principle, the first two bets agree on yellow (both pay 0), and the last two are those same two bets with the yellow payoff raised to 100 for both; yellow is a shared payoff within each pair, so it should cancel, and the red-versus-black ranking should carry over to the (red-or-yellow)-versus-(black-or-yellow) ranking. The observed choices reverse it. Equivalently, preferring the bet on red requires \(P(\text{red}) > P(\text{black})\), while preferring the bet on black-or-yellow requires \(P(\text{black}) > P(\text{red})\); no prior satisfies both. The preferences are stable and widely shared, yet no single prior represents them — the gap the objection points to. This ambiguity aversion is reproducible and arguably rational, so it places such preferences outside the scope of Savage’s theorem: “I cannot fix a sharp prior” is then a position the axioms do not exclude, not a confusion about probability.
The orthodox reply is to add a level. If the composition of the urn is unknown, put a prior over it — and in this symmetric problem any prior that treats black and yellow alike forces the predictive probabilities to \(P(\text{red}) = P(\text{black}) = P(\text{yellow}) = 1/3\), whereupon the ambiguity disappears and the problem reduces to ordinary risk. This is de Finetti’s reduction: beliefs about an unknown frequency, weighted by a prior over its values, collapse to a single predictive distribution. The move is available, and here the choice of second-order prior does not even matter, because symmetry fixes the answer. Two things limit it. First, the reduced model predicts indifference between the urns, which is not what people do; it recommends against the phenomenon rather than accounting for it. Second, the symmetry is special — in an asymmetric problem the predictive probabilities depend on the parametrisation of the “ignorance” prior, the difficulty the objective-Bayes section already noted. Whether ambiguity may always be reduced to risk in this way is the contested step, and the models below take the other branch.


8.6.3 Sets of priors: imprecise probability and robust Bayes
If a single sharp prior overstates what is known, the response that keeps the calculus is to carry a set of priors rather than one. A closed set of distributions — a credal set — assigns each event a lower and an upper probability, \(\underline P(A) = \inf_p p(A)\) and \(\overline P(A) = \sup_p p(A)\) over the set; the width \(\overline P(A) - \underline P(A)\) records how little is known, and is zero only when the set collapses to a point and probability becomes precise. Total ignorance is the vacuous set, \(\underline P(A) = 0\) and \(\overline P(A) = 1\) — which is what ignorance looks like, in contrast to the uniform prior, a definite symmetric commitment that the objective-Bayes section warned against confusing with it.
Two traditions develop this with the same mathematics and different emphasis. Imprecise probability rebuilds the foundations: where de Finetti’s agent posts one fair price for a gamble, Walley’s agent posts two — a highest buying price and a lowest selling price — and declines to trade in between, so the betting argument of Road 1 generalises by dropping the assumption that every gamble has a single fair price.48 A concrete instance is the imprecise Dirichlet model for proportions, which begins vacuous and contracts as data accumulate.49 Robust Bayes keeps ordinary Bayes but, conceding that one prior cannot be pinned down, specifies a class of priors, recomputes the posterior quantity for each, and reports the range; a narrow range means the conclusion is insensitive to the prior, a wide one that the data do not determine it.50 This is the global form of the sensitivity analysis the chapter has already endorsed. A decision still has to be made from a set, and one rule is maxmin expected utility: score each option by its expected utility under the least favourable prior in the set — its worst case over the priors entertained — and choose the option whose worst case is best.51 In Ellsberg’s urn this reproduces the preference for known odds, because a bet on a known colour has a value every prior agrees on, whereas a bet on an unknown colour is judged by the composition least favourable to it. A separate limit is worth keeping in view: every guarantee here holds relative to the set of models entertained, and if the data-generating process lies outside all of them, coherence no longer ensures the conclusion is correct.52


8.6.4 Dilation
Carrying a set of priors has a consequence with no analogue in single-prior analysis, and it bears directly on later chapters. Ordinarily, data narrow beliefs. With a set of priors, conditioning on an observation can widen the interval: for some partitions one can know in advance that, whichever cell is observed, the posterior interval for a proposition will be wider than the prior interval. This is dilation.53
A fair coin is to be tossed, so the probability of heads is \(1/2\). A second person announces a prediction of the toss, but nothing is known of their reliability — the credal set admits everything from a perfect predictor to a perfect anti-predictor. Before the prediction is revealed the probability of heads is \(1/2\); after it is revealed, the conditional probability of heads ranges over the whole interval from near 0 to near 1, because the set contains distributions under which the prediction is highly informative in either direction. An uninterpretable signal from a source of unknown reliability widens a probability that was previously sharp, and one could have foreseen that any prediction would do so.
Dilation is not an inconsistency: the model stays coherent, and no sure loss can be made against it. Whether it is a defect or a virtue is disputed. Read as a defect, an inference that becomes less certain on data looks pathological. Read as a virtue, the precise \(1/2\) was the artefact — it relied on an unstated assumption that the prediction was independent of the coin, and once that assumption is withdrawn the wide interval is the faithful report. The phenomenon also corrects a natural assumption about robust Bayes: because robust Bayes updates a set of priors by the same rule, it dilates too. Where a robust-Bayes analysis shows no dilation, it is because the class was anchored tightly to an informative base prior — that is, more was assumed than the radical-uncertainty objection grants. One cannot claim both deep ignorance, which requires a wide set, and immunity from dilation, which requires a narrow one.
The phenomenon has a direct counterpart in applied work. When the sign or magnitude of a bias — unmeasured confounding, an unknown selection mechanism — is genuinely not known, an analysis that represents that ignorance faithfully can yield bounds the data fail to narrow, and that may widen on further conditioning. This is the logic of partial identification and of the sensitivity analyses developed in Chapter 19; dilation is the same fact stated at the level of belief.


8.6.5 Is ambiguity aversion irrational?
The biases catalogued in Chapter 2 — base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy, anchoring — are departures from probability or expected-utility theory that people renounce once the structure is pointed out. It is tempting to file ambiguity aversion alongside them, as one more failure to reason coherently. There is a strong argument for doing so, due to Raiffa: if you are indifferent between betting on red and betting on black in the unknown urn, decide the colour by a fair coin; the resulting mixture has a known one-half chance of paying, matching the known urn, so a coherent agent should not prefer one urn to the other.54 On this view ambiguity aversion forgoes a sure equivalence, and it does attenuate with incentives and learning.
Two features distinguish it from the Chapter 2 biases. It survives reflection: sophisticated agents shown the argument frequently continue to prefer known odds and defend the preference, whereas the mark of a fallacy is that one abandons it once it is seen. And it has been given normative, not merely descriptive, axiomatisations — Choquet expected utility55, maxmin expected utility56, and smooth-ambiguity preferences57 are theories of rational choice that weaken the sure-thing principle deliberately, and it has been argued that committing to a precise prior one has no information to justify is itself the less rational course.58 Whether ambiguity aversion is irrational therefore turns on whether Savage’s axioms are taken as constitutive of rationality or as one model of it — and this book has already taken the modest view, that probability theory captures an important part of rational thinking rather than the whole of it. On that view the cleaner classification is not that ambiguity aversion fails to meet the standard, but that it disputes which standard applies.


8.6.6 The position taken here
None of these challenges refutes the calculus; each bounds the scope of one way of using it. Single-event probabilities are meaningful and are validated over many forecasts, not one. Under radical uncertainty a sharp prior may not be available, and a set of priors with a stated decision rule is the disciplined response, at the price of phenomena such as dilation. Ambiguity aversion is better read as a rival standard than as a mistake. For the work in this book — finite data, models with declared structure, priors that must survive criticism and sensitivity analysis — a single prior, varied and checked, is adequate, and is what the later chapters use; the apparatus of sets of priors is held in reserve for the cases, flagged where they arise, in which a single prior would assert more than is known. The aim is unchanged from the chapter’s first page: to quantify the uncertainty that can be quantified, and to mark plainly the uncertainty that cannot.

8  What probability means, and the robot

title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
text:
8.7 Key points

The calculus is forced twice over, by two independent routes. Chapter 5 reached the sum and product rules by counting; this chapter reaches the same rules from the robot’s desiderata (Cox) and from the requirement of no sure loss on graded commitments (the Dutch book). That counting and consistency deliver one calculus is the main reason to take it seriously as the logic of science.
The chapter’s first half concerns what the number means: probability is read as epistemic (a degree of belief) rather than aleatoric (a physical property of a repeatable set-up), because the epistemic reading keeps working for single cases and unique hypotheses where the frequency reading falls silent.
Probability attaches to propositions, so it is always the two-place \(P(A \mid I)\); reading the number as a property of the world is the mind-projection fallacy. The sample space is fixed by the experiment; the hypothesis space \(\mathcal{H}\) — the set of explanations the analyst entertains, each a probability law over \(\Omega\) rather than an event in it — is fixed by the analyst, and every posterior is a relative plausibility within the current \(\mathcal{H}\), never an absolute verdict. Conditioning redistributes mass within \(\mathcal{H}\) and can kill a hypothesis (zero likelihood), but only revision of \(\mathcal{H}\) can create one; embedding \(\mathcal{H}\) in a grand sample space of (hypothesis, outcome) pairs makes Bayes literal pebble-conditioning but freezes with the list it was built from. Model criticism is how the hypothesis space learns.
The whole calculus is two rules: the sum rule \(P(A) + P(\lnot A) = 1\) and the product rule \(P(A \land B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)\).
The called-off bet is the operational meaning of conditional probability: a commitment about B activated only when A turns out true — the three-valued structure of Chapter 3’s historical aside, put to work.
The calculus keeps Chapter 3’s promises: at probabilities 0 and 1 it reproduces the strong syllogisms, and it licenses the weak ones quantitatively — if A entails B, then \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)/P(B) \geq P(A)\).
Counting is the symmetric special case of the belief calculus: when information does not distinguish a finite set of cases, desideratum 3.3 makes them equally probable, and probability reduces to favourable-over-possible.
Additivity (axiom 3) requires mutual exclusivity, not independence.
The fine print of the agreement: Cox’s theorem needs technical assumptions, and the belief road forces only finite — not countable — additivity. The roads also differ on what carries probability (propositions and single cases vs repeatable setups). None of this affects the working rules used in this book.
Within the epistemic reading, the subjective school (Ramsey, de Finetti, Savage) requires only coherence and expects agreement to emerge from shared data, while the objective school (Jeffreys, Jaynes) requires that the same information yield the same probability, and supplies symmetry, invariance, and maximum-entropy rules for the assignment. The dispute concerns where prior probabilities come from; both schools deny that probability is physical.
Pushed to its ideal limit — a prior over all computable hypotheses, updated without resource limit — the robot becomes Solomonoff induction (and, for an agent that also acts, AIXI): a provably optimal predictor that is nonetheless (i) only coherence-optimal, not truth-optimal — a misspecified model converges confidently to the pseudo-true value; (ii) able to update within a hypothesis space but never to enlarge it (the problem of new hypotheses); and (iii) uncomputable, so every real system — a large pretrained model included — is a resource-bounded approximation. The robot moves through a space of hypotheses; it does not make the space.
The Bayesian position faces genuine challenges as well as misunderstandings. A single-event probability is meaningful but is validated only over many forecasts, through calibration. Under radical uncertainty a sharp prior may not be elicitable, and Ellsberg’s experiment exhibits reproducible ambiguity aversion that violates Savage’s sure-thing principle, so no single prior represents the preferences. The disciplined response carries a set of priors (imprecise probability, robust Bayes) with a decision rule such as maxmin expected utility — at the cost of dilation, in which conditioning can widen rather than narrow the interval. These bound the scope of the single-prior workflow without refuting the calculus.

title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
text:
8.8 Exercises

Make your own Dutch book. A colleague prices a ticket on A at 0.60 and a ticket on NOT A at 0.55. Construct the trades that guarantee the colleague a loss, and compute the loss. Then do the same for prices 0.30 and 0.50 (note the direction of trade reverses).
The second weak syllogism. Suppose A entails B (\(P(B \mid A) = 1\)), with \(0 < P(A) < 1\) and \(P(B) < 1\). Using the decomposition \(P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid \lnot A)P(\lnot A)\), show that \(P(B \mid \lnot A) \leq P(B)\): learning that A is false makes B less plausible. State the condition under which the inequality is strict.
Extend the mini-sim. For the clinic example, compute the probability that at least one of the two selected patients is a carrier, three ways: by counting (complement of choosing both from the 7 non-carriers), by the sum and product rules, and by extending the Monte Carlo chunk. Confirm the three answers agree.
Conditional probabilities in the cohort. Source R/simulate_cohort.R and generate the master cohort. By counting rows, estimate \(P(\text{stroke} \mid \text{drug})\) and \(P(\text{stroke} \mid \lnot\text{drug})\), and verify the product rule numerically: \(P(\text{stroke} \land \text{drug}) = P(\text{drug}) \cdot P(\text{stroke} \mid \text{drug})\). These conditional probabilities are associational quantities; why they must not be read as the effect of the drug is the subject of Chapters 4 and 10.
The single case. The forecast says there is a 70% chance of rain tomorrow. Explain what this number means on the belief road and what auxiliary construction the counting road needs to make sense of it. Which parts of the construction are testable?
The called-off bet, reversed. An agent prices \(P(A) = 0.5\), \(P(A \land B) = 0.2\), but the conditional ticket on “B given A” at \(q = 0.3\) (the coherent price is 0.4). Adapt the Dutch book chunk to construct the sure loss against this agent, and verify that the loss per unit equals \(P(A \land B) - q \cdot P(A)\).
The second-order prior in Ellsberg’s urn. Take the 90-ball urn (30 red; 60 black or yellow, unknown split). Put a prior on the number of black balls that is symmetric in black and yellow, and show that the predictive probabilities are \(P(\text{red}) = P(\text{black}) = P(\text{yellow}) = 1/3\), so an expected-utility agent is indifferent within each pair of bets in the table. State which empirical fact this prediction fails to match, and name a decision rule that reproduces the observed preference for known odds.
Dilation. In the coin-and-predictor example, explain why learning the prediction widens the interval for “heads” from the point \(1/2\) to almost all of \([0, 1]\), and identify the single assumption a precise-prior analysis would have to add to keep the probability at \(1/2\). Does robust Bayes avoid the widening, and why?
The limits of the universal thinker. A colleague argues: “Give a Bayesian machine a prior over every computable hypothesis and unlimited compute, and it will eventually think every thought worth thinking.” Using the three limits set out in this chapter, write a short reply. (a) In what sense is such a machine provably optimal, and in what sense is that optimality merely conditional? (b) Explain why conditioning on more data cannot, by itself, give non-zero probability to a hypothesis the prior excluded, and name one historical concept whose introduction would have required exactly that move. (c) State the result that makes the ideal machine physically unrealisable, and say what it implies about the relation between real AI systems and the ideal.

title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
text:
“Reports that say that something hasn’t happened are always interesting to me, because as we know, there are known knowns; there are things we know we know. We also know there are known unknowns; that is to say we know there are some things we do not know. But there are also unknown unknowns - the ones we don’t know we don’t know. And if one looks throughout the history of our country and other free countries, it is the latter category that tends to be the difficult ones.” Donald Rumsfeld (US Secretary of Defence, 2002)↩︎
It is a thorny question, how fundamentally these uncertainties really differ from each other. Here we take the strong view that ultimately all uncertainties that matter (with the possible exception of quantum mechanics) are epistemic, meaning that they are in our heads. For example, if we could see every atom, every electron in the cell, we could perhaps predict every mutation and lose the randomness from biological variation↩︎
Lam R, Sanchez-Gonzalez A, Willson M, Wirnsberger P, Fortunato M, Alet F, et al., “Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting,” Science 2023;382:1416-1422 (DOI).↩︎
Price I, Sanchez-Gonzalez A, Alet F, Andersson TR, El-Kadi A, Masters D, et al., “Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning,” Nature 2024;637:84-90 (DOI).↩︎
de Finetti opens the Preface with “PROBABILITY DOES NOT EXIST”, grouping the objective conception of probability with the abandoned fictions of phlogiston, the cosmic ether, absolute space and time, and fairies and witches. de Finetti B, Theory of Probability: A Critical Introductory Treatment, Vol. 1 (trans. Machí A, Smith A), London: Wiley, 1974 (Preface, p. x).↩︎
Hacking I, The Emergence of Probability: A Philosophical Study of Early Ideas about Probability, Induction and Statistical Inference, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1975 (2nd ed. 2006).↩︎
Venn J, The Logic of Chance, London: Macmillan, 1866; von Mises R, Probability, Statistics and Truth, 2nd revised English ed. (prepared by Geiringer H), London: Allen & Unwin, 1957 (German original Wahrscheinlichkeit, Statistik und Wahrheit, Vienna: Springer, 1928); Reichenbach H, The Theory of Probability, trans. Hutten EH, Reichenbach M, Berkeley: University of California Press, 1949 (German original Wahrscheinlichkeitslehre, Leiden: Sijthoff, 1935). A survey of the frequency and propensity theories and their difficulties is Gillies D, Philosophical Theories of Probability, London: Routledge, 2000.↩︎
Popper KR, “The Propensity Interpretation of Probability,” Br J Philos Sci 1959;10:25-42.↩︎
Humphreys P, “Why Propensities Cannot Be Probabilities,” Philos Rev 1985;94:557-570. The difficulty, now called Humphreys’s paradox, is that the multiplication axiom and Bayes’ theorem require the inverse conditional \(P(\text{condition} \mid \text{outcome})\) to exist and behave as a probability, whereas a propensity is a time-directed causal disposition for which that inverse has no interpretation; subsequent work has explored weakening either the axioms or the propensity reading rather than abandoning one.↩︎
Comte A, Cours de philosophie positive, Paris: Bachelier, 1830-1842; von Mises R, Positivism: A Study in Human Understanding, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1951 (German original Kleines Lehrbuch des Positivismus, The Hague: Van Stockum, 1939). Reichenbach co-founded the Berlin Society for Empirical Philosophy, the logical-empiricist group allied with the Vienna Circle.↩︎
Fisher RA, Statistical Methods for Research Workers, Edinburgh: Oliver & Boyd, 1925; Neyman J, Pearson ES, “On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses,” Philos Trans R Soc Lond A 1933;231:289-337 (DOI); Neyman J, “Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability,” Philos Trans R Soc Lond A 1937;236:333-380 (DOI) — the origin of the confidence interval.↩︎
Jaynes ET, Probability Theory: The Logic of Science (Bretthorst GL, ed.), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003. The fallacy — attributing to the world what belongs to the reasoner’s state of knowledge — is a recurring theme of the book.↩︎
Jaynes ET, Probability Theory: The Logic of Science (Bretthorst GL, ed.), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003 (ch. 4, on multiple hypothesis testing, where surprising data revive hypotheses that were given negligible standing at the outset).↩︎
The name is Lindley’s, after Cromwell’s 1650 plea to the Church of Scotland (“think it possible you may be mistaken”): Lindley DV, Making Decisions, 2nd ed., London: Wiley, 1985.↩︎
Savage LJ, The Foundations of Statistics, New York: Wiley, 1954 (2nd revised ed. New York: Dover, 1972). Ramsey’s and de Finetti’s foundational papers are cited in the Dutch book section below.↩︎
Blackwell D, Dubins L, “Merging of Opinions with Increasing Information,” Ann Math Statist 1962;33:882-886 (DOI). The result requires the two priors to be mutually absolutely continuous; where they are mutually singular on an event — as a continuous and a spike-and-slab prior are on \(\{\theta = 0\}\) — it does not apply there.↩︎
Lindley DV, “A Statistical Paradox,” Biometrika 1957;44:187-192 (DOI); Bartlett MS, “A comment on D. V. Lindley’s statistical paradox,” Biometrika 1957;44:533-534 (DOI). The Bayesian point-null test, and the dependence of its verdict on the slab, originate with Jeffreys H, Theory of Probability, 3rd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1961.↩︎
Jaynes ET, “Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics,” Phys Rev 1957;106:620-630 (DOI); Jaynes ET, “Prior Probabilities,” IEEE Trans Syst Sci Cybern 1968;4:227-241 (DOI).↩︎
Long-run betting performance measures neither; it tracks calibration, an external standard. It happens to correlate with the objectivist’s extra clause, which is why a wager seems to favour the better-calibrated agent — but the subjectivist bites the bullet that a rational agent can be coherent, well-reasoned by its own lights, and still lose.↩︎
The non-uniqueness is structural, not merely practical. Parametrisation. The principle of indifference is not invariant under a change of variable: a density that is flat in a parameter is not flat in its square or its logarithm, so the instruction to give indistinguishable cases equal probability returns different answers according to how the cases are described. The classical demonstration is Bertrand’s chord problem, in which three equally natural descriptions of a “random” chord yield three different probabilities (Bertrand J, Calcul des probabilités, Paris: Gauthier-Villars, 1889); Jaynes’s transformation-group rule resolves such a problem only where the stated information carries a definite symmetry. Constraints and reference measure. Maximum entropy removes the ambiguity only after the analyst has fixed which constraints to impose and, on a continuous space, a reference measure against which entropy is defined; different admissible choices give different priors, and neither is determined by the information. The Jeffreys prior is invariant under reparametrisation — that is its purpose — but is computed from the Fisher information, a feature of the sampling model, so it depends on which experiment produced the data rather than on the parameter alone. Coherence. The priors these rules produce are frequently improper, and impropriety can generate the marginalisation paradox, in which two valid derivations of the same posterior quantity disagree (Dawid AP, Stone M, Zidek JV, “Marginalization Paradoxes in Bayesian and Structural Inference,” J R Stat Soc Series B 1973;35:189-233 (DOI)). The attempt to fix a prior by rule can therefore conflict with the coherence requirement both schools accept. None of this makes objective priors useless: where the information carries a genuine symmetry they are well defined and command wide agreement. It shows only that “the information fixes the prior” holds in special cases, not as a general rule.↩︎
Reference priors derive a default by maximising the information the data are expected to supply about the parameter, so that the prior’s own contribution is minimal (Bernardo JM, “Reference Posterior Distributions for Bayesian Inference,” J R Stat Soc Series B 1979;41:113-147 (DOI)). Weakly informative priors instead impose deliberately mild bounds that exclude implausible values and regularise the estimate without encoding specific subject-matter knowledge (Gelman A, Jakulin A, Pittau MG, Su YS, “A Weakly Informative Default Prior Distribution for Logistic and Other Regression Models,” Ann Appl Stat 2008;2:1360-1383 (DOI)). For the argument that the subjective/objective division is itself too coarse to classify these practices, see Gelman A, Hennig C, “Beyond Subjective and Objective in Statistics,” J R Stat Soc Series A 2017;180:967-1033 (DOI).↩︎
Two examples show what “deriving” a prior means. Invariance. Suppose the parameter \(\sigma\) is a scale — a standard deviation, say — and the stated information does not include the units of measurement. A prior that carries no information about scale must then have the same form whether \(\sigma\) is recorded in days or in hours, i.e. its shape must not change when \(\sigma\) is multiplied by a positive constant. The only density with this property is \(p(\sigma) \propto 1/\sigma\), which is a flat prior on \(\log \sigma\). Jeffreys generalised this style of argument into a rule — the Jeffreys prior, proportional to the square root of the Fisher information — which returns the same posterior whichever smooth transformation of the parameter the analyst works with (Jeffreys H, “An invariant form for the prior probability in estimation problems,” Proc R Soc Lond A Math Phys Sci 1946;186:453-461 (DOI)). Maximum entropy. The entropy of a distribution is a single number measuring how spread out the distribution is — equivalently, how little it commits to beyond what is stated. The rule is: express the available information as constraints, then adopt the distribution with the largest entropy among all distributions satisfying those constraints; any other choice encodes information that was not stated. Three standard results. With no constraints beyond a finite list of possible outcomes, the maximum-entropy distribution is the uniform — the symmetry argument recovered as a special case. For a positive quantity with a stated mean, it is the exponential distribution. For a quantity on the real line with stated mean and variance, it is the normal distribution. (These distributions are introduced in Chapter 6.)↩︎
O’Hagan A, “Expert Knowledge Elicitation: Subjective but Scientific,” Am Stat 2019;73:69-81 (DOI); a book-length treatment of the methodology is O’Hagan A, Buck CE, Daneshkhah A, Eiser JR, Garthwaite PH, Jenkinson DJ, Oakley JE, Rakow T, Uncertain Judgements: Eliciting Experts’ Probabilities, Chichester: Wiley, 2006.↩︎
Genest C, Zidek JV, “Combining Probability Distributions: A Critique and an Annotated Bibliography,” Statist Sci 1986;1:114-135 (DOI).↩︎
Quantum mechanics describes a physical system by a mathematical object called the quantum state (in the simplest case a wave function, \(\psi\)). The state evolves deterministically in time, according to the Schrödinger equation; probability enters the theory at a single point, when a measurement is made. The Born rule states that the quantum state attaches to each possible measurement outcome a complex number, the amplitude, and that the probability of an outcome is the squared magnitude of its amplitude. The rule is a separate postulate — it does not follow from the rest of the formalism — and it is the source of every probability that quantum theory predicts; those predictions are among the most precisely confirmed in physics. The interpretations of quantum mechanics differ on what the rule’s probabilities are: a physical propensity of the system, a relative frequency across branching worlds, or — the QBist reading — a normative constraint on the beliefs of the agent who measures. Born M, “Zur Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge,” Z Phys 1926;37:863-867 (DOI).↩︎
Caves CM, Fuchs CA, Schack R, “Quantum probabilities as Bayesian probabilities,” Phys Rev A 2002;65:022305 (DOI); Fuchs CA, Mermin ND, Schack R, “An introduction to QBism with an application to the locality of quantum mechanics,” Am J Phys 2014;82:749-754 (DOI). A book-length account for the general reader, without equations: von Baeyer HC, QBism: The Future of Quantum Physics, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2016.↩︎
Mermin ND, “Physics: QBism puts the scientist back into science,” Nature 2014;507:421-423 (DOI); Fuchs CA, “On Participatory Realism,” in Durham IT, Rickles D (eds.), Information and Interaction: Eddington, Wheeler, and the Limits of Knowledge, Cham: Springer, 2017:113-134 (DOI).↩︎
Jaynes ET, Probability Theory: The Logic of Science (Bretthorst GL, ed.), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003 (chapters 1–2).↩︎
Cox RT, “Probability, frequency and reasonable expectation,” Am J Phys 1946;14:1-13 (DOI).↩︎
Ramsey FP, “Truth and Probability” (written 1926), in Braithwaite RB (ed.), The Foundations of Mathematics and other Logical Essays, London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1931:156-198; de Finetti B, “La prévision: ses lois logiques, ses sources subjectives,” Ann Inst Henri Poincaré 1937;7:1-68 (text).↩︎
There are two grades of 3.3. (i) Coherence-grade: Logically equivalent propositions get the same number. Violating it is a Dutch book and therefore both schools accept it. As a Dutch book is made against an individual’s book, never against a pair of people, coherence is a one-person predicate. (ii) Indifference-grade: Symmetric information leads to equal probabilities. (technically, Your information is symmetric with respect to a transformation when: (a) the transformation maps the hypothesis space onto itself, and (b) your state of knowledge \(I\) is left invariant by it.) This is Jaynes’s bridge to maximum entropy which, alas, is contestable even for one actor. This reading would force agreement across actors. The subjectivist seeks inter-actor agreement as an instrumental good (a committee must act on one distribution; reproducibility; pooling partly-independent judgements improves calibration), and reaches it two ways: (a) Convergence by conditioning on shared data — the prior washes out. (b) Elicitation / pooling, which is a negotiated consensus. Thus, disagreement is not a defect of rationality but a coordination inconvenience, and a signal for a need to get more data. The subjectivist can call a badly-reasoned prior poorly-calibrated or unwise, but not irrational (that word is reserved for incoherence). While many find that taxonomy too thin, the objectivists make agreement a norm but cannot supply the unique prior the norm requires. This drives people past the dichotomy — Gelman & Hennig’s “Beyond subjective and objective in statistics” replaces the subjective/objective with virtues both camps can own: transparency about assumptions, calibration, robustness.↩︎
van Fraassen BC, Laws and Symmetry, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1989 (the cube factory).↩︎
The problem is due to Bertrand J, Calcul des probabilités, Paris: Gauthier-Villars, 1889; the invariance resolution is Jaynes ET, “The Well-Posed Problem,” Found Phys 1973;3:477-493 (DOI).↩︎
Van Horn KS, “Constructing a logic of plausible inference: a guide to Cox’s theorem,” Int J Approx Reason 2003;34:3-24.↩︎
Solomonoff RJ, “A formal theory of inductive inference. Part I,” Inf Control 1964;7:1-22; “Part II,” Inf Control 1964;7:224-254. The decision-theoretic extension, to an agent that acts as well as predicts, is AIXI: Hutter M, Universal Artificial Intelligence: Sequential Decisions Based on Algorithmic Probability, Berlin: Springer, 2005.↩︎
Berk RH, “Limiting behavior of posterior distributions when the model is incorrect,” Ann Math Statist 1966;37:51-58 (DOI). When the true distribution is not in the model class, the posterior concentrates on the member of the class minimising the Kullback–Leibler divergence to the truth — the pseudo-true value.↩︎
The classical consistency theorem is Doob JL, “Application of the theory of martingales,” in Le Calcul des Probabilités et ses Applications, Paris: CNRS, 1949:23-27; the Bernstein–von Mises theorem and the consistency theory are set out in van der Vaart AW, Asymptotic Statistics, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998 (ch. 10). Cromwell’s rule — that a prior of 0 or 1 is never revised by any evidence — is due to Lindley DV, Making Decisions, 2nd ed., London: Wiley, 1985. The merging-of-opinions result is Blackwell and Dubins, cited in the point-null discussion above.↩︎
That Bayesian conditionalisation redistributes probability among the hypotheses already entertained, and has no rule for enlarging its own space, is the problem of new hypotheses (or new theories): Glymour C, Theory and Evidence, Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1980; Earman J, Bayes or Bust? A Critical Examination of Bayesian Confirmation Theory, Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1992 (ch. 5).↩︎
Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable — evaluating it reduces to the halting problem — so Solomonoff’s universal prior and AIXI are uncomputable; see Li M, Vitányi P, An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications, 4th ed., Cham: Springer, 2019. Even for a computable model class, exact probabilistic inference over a rich space is intractable: Roth D, “On the hardness of approximate reasoning,” Artif Intell 1996;82:273-302 (DOI), which shows the relevant counting problems are #P-hard.↩︎
The assumption at issue is logical omniscience; the attempt to model a reasoner uncertain about the consequences of its own axioms is Garrabrant S, Benson-Tilsen T, Critch A, Soares N, Taylor J, “Logical Induction,” arXiv:1609.03543, 2016. This is distinct from, and does not depend on, the Lucas–Penrose argument that Gödel’s theorems show human minds are not machines (Lucas JR, “Minds, Machines and Gödel,” Philosophy 1961;36:112-127; Penrose R, The Emperor’s New Mind, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1989), which is widely regarded as an overreach.↩︎
Xie SM, Raghunathan A, Liang P, Ma T, “An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference,” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2022 (arXiv:2111.02080). The claim is that a model pretrained on data with long-range structure performs, at inference time, something close to Bayesian averaging over a latent concept — within the hypothesis space fixed at pretraining.↩︎
Brier GW, “Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability,” Mon Weather Rev 1950;78:1-3; Dawid AP, “The Well-Calibrated Bayesian,” J Am Stat Assoc 1982;77:605-610 (DOI).↩︎
Knight FH, Risk, Uncertainty and Profit, Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1921.↩︎
Keynes JM, A Treatise on Probability, London: Macmillan, 1921.↩︎
Kay J, King M, Radical Uncertainty: Decision-Making Beyond the Numbers, New York: W. W. Norton, 2020.↩︎
A simple case. Two set dinners differ only by a coin toss. Menu A serves soup on heads and ice cream on tails; Menu B serves fish on heads and ice cream on tails. Both serve ice cream on tails, so tails cannot settle the choice — you should prefer A to B just as you prefer soup to fish. The sure-thing principle adds that this ranking is unchanged if the shared tails course is swapped, say for cake: altering a payoff common to both menus, in the state where they already agree, leaves the comparison untouched. Savage’s original illustration was a businessman who would buy a property whether an election went one way or the other, and so need not wait for the result.↩︎
Ellsberg D, “Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms,” Q J Econ 1961;75:643-669 (DOI).↩︎
Walley P, Statistical Reasoning with Imprecise Probabilities, London: Chapman and Hall, 1991.↩︎
For a proportion estimated from counts, ordinary Bayes uses a single Beta prior, which may be written through a prior strength \(s > 0\) and a prior mean \(t\); after \(a\) successes in \(n\) trials the posterior mean is \((a + st)/(n + s)\). The imprecise Dirichlet model fixes \(s\) but lets the prior mean \(t\) range over the whole interval \((0, 1)\) — a set of priors in place of one — and reports the resulting range. The lower and upper probabilities for the category are then \(a/(n + s)\) and \((a + s)/(n + s)\). With no data (\(n = 0\)) these are \(0\) and \(1\), the vacuous interval; as \(n\) grows both converge to the observed frequency \(a/n\) while the width \(s/(n + s)\) shrinks to zero, so the imprecision contracts at the rate information arrives. Walley P, “Inferences from Multinomial Data: Learning About a Bag of Marbles,” J R Stat Soc Series B 1996;58:3-34 (DOI).↩︎

The urn fixes the credal set: \(P(\text{red}) = 1/3\), while \(P(\text{black})\) ranges over \([0, 2/3]\) and \(P(\text{yellow}) = 2/3 - P(\text{black})\). With the table’s £100/£0 payoffs each bet’s expected value is £100 times its chance of paying, so the ranking follows the win-probabilities. The bet on red pays with probability \(1/3\) under every prior, so its worst case is \(1/3\); the bet on black pays with probability \(P(\text{black})\), whose worst case over the set is \(0\) — so maxmin ranks red above black. For the wider bets, “black or yellow” pays with probability \(2/3\) under every prior (worst case \(2/3\)), while “red or yellow” pays with probability \(1 - P(\text{black})\), worst case \(1/3\) — so maxmin ranks “black or yellow” above “red or yellow”. 8  What probability means, and the robot

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.1 Prior, likelihood, and posterior
Prior probability \(P(\text{Hypothesis})\) is a purely logical term that incorporates all relevant evidence that is not present in the data. The separation of evidence into “data” and “prior” is a matter of convenience of calculation, nothing more.
Likelihood \(P(\text{data} \vert \text{Hypothesis})\) models how probable the sample data are for each member of the sample space. If \(\Omega =\{H_1,H_2\}\), then the likelihood has two members as well: \(P(\text{data} \vert H_1)\) is the probability of seeing the sample data if it happens that \(H_1\) is true, and \(P(\text{data} \vert H_2)\) is the probability of seeing the sample data if it happens that \(H_2\) is true. If the likelihood ratio \(LR = \frac{P(\text{data} \vert H_1)}{P(\text{data} \vert H_2)} = 1\), then the data are irrelevant. \(LR = 10\) means that the data support \(H_1\) ten times more than \(H_2\).
The fact that the sample data provide much more evidence for \(H_1\) than for \(H_2\) does not by itself mean that we should think \(H_1\) more probable than \(H_2\), or than any other logically possible hypothesis. Likelihoods do not sum to one over the sample space. Therefore likelihood is not a probability.
Posterior probability \(P(\text{Hypothesis} \vert \text{data} \,\&\, \text{prior})\) is the product of prior and likelihood over each member of the sample space, normalised so that the probabilities sum to one over the sample space. The posterior distribution is the output of Bayesian inference: the probability distribution that holds our beliefs about the parameter values, after the data.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.2 The Bayes theorem
We can derive Bayes’ theorem straight from the definition of conditional probability (Chapter 5),
\[P(A\vert B) = \frac{P(A \land B)}{P(B)},\]
and equivalently \[P(B\vert A) = \frac{P(B \land A)}{P(A)}.\]
As \(P(A \land B) = P(B \land A)\),
\[P(A\vert B)\,P(B) = P(B\vert A)\,P(A),\] and so
\[P(A\vert B) =\frac{P(A)\,P(B\vert A)}{P(B)}.\] This is Bayes’ theorem. Now let us substitute hypothesis \(H\) for \(A\) and data \(d\) for \(B\):
\[P(H \vert d) =\frac{P(H)\,P(d\vert H)}{P(d)}.\] Here \(P(H\vert d)\) is the posterior, \(P(H)\) is the prior probability of the hypothesis, \(P(d\vert H)\) is the likelihood (the probability of the data given the hypothesis), and \(P(d)\) is the total probability of the data, summed over all the hypotheses in the sample space. \(P(d)\) is the normalising constant, which guarantees that the posterior probabilities sum to one over the sample space.
The single most important thing to remember is that the posterior is proportional to the product of prior and likelihood.
What does \(P(d)\) really mean? If \(\Omega = \{H, \lnot H \}\), then
\[P(d) = P(d \land H) + P(d \land \lnot H) = P(H)P(d\vert H) + P(\lnot H)P(d\vert \lnot H),\]
where the final step comes from the definition of conditional probability.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
section: 9.3 The odds form: prior odds, likelihood ratio, posterior odds
text:
9.3 The odds form: prior odds, likelihood ratio, posterior odds
The normalising constant \(P(d)\) is the same for every hypothesis in the sample space, which is the source of a great simplification. Write Bayes’ theorem for two hypotheses, \(H_1\) and \(H_2\), and divide one by the other. The \(P(d)\) cancels:
\[\underbrace{\frac{P(H_1\vert d)}{P(H_2\vert d)}}_{\text{posterior odds}}
= \underbrace{\frac{P(H_1)}{P(H_2)}}_{\text{prior odds}}
   \times
   \underbrace{\frac{P(d\vert H_1)}{P(d\vert H_2)}}_{\text{likelihood ratio}}.\]
In words: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. This is Bayes’ theorem in its most useful form. It separates cleanly into the two ingredients of an inference — the prior odds, which carry everything known before the data, and the likelihood ratio, which carries everything the data contribute. The likelihood ratio (for two simple hypotheses, the Bayes factor) is the multiplicative factor by which the data shift the odds. It is the quantitative form of the weak syllogism from Chapter 7: evidence is not “for” a hypothesis in isolation but always relative to a named alternative.
Three consequences follow immediately, and each is a recurring theme of the book:

Evidence is comparative. \(P(d\vert H_1)\) on its own moves nothing; only its ratio to \(P(d\vert H_2)\) does. A hypothesis can be confirmed only against a stated rival.
A small likelihood ratio cannot rescue a small prior, and a large prior cannot be ignored. Both factors multiply.
The prior is unavoidable. Refusing to state one does not remove it; it only hides the prior odds you have implicitly assumed.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.4 The weight of evidence
Multiplying odds across several independent pieces of evidence is awkward. Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum. Define the weight of evidence as the logarithm of the likelihood ratio,
\[W = \log \frac{P(d\vert H_1)}{P(d\vert H_2)},\]
so that Bayes’ theorem in odds form becomes additive:
\[\log(\text{posterior odds}) = \log(\text{prior odds}) + W.\]
Evidence now behaves like a physical quantity that accumulates: two independent experiments contribute weights \(W_1\) and \(W_2\), and the total evidence is \(W_1 + W_2\). This formulation, and the term “weight of evidence”, are due to I. J. Good, building on wartime work with Alan Turing; in base-ten logarithms the unit is the ban, and one tenth of a ban is the deciban, the smallest change in the plausibility of a hypothesis a person can reasonably perceive.1 Positive weight favours \(H_1\), negative weight favours \(H_2\), and zero weight (likelihood ratio 1) is data that cannot tell the two hypotheses apart — a case that returns, decisively, in the Madame Marie example below.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
section: 9.5 A worked example: a diagnostic test
text:
9.5 A worked example: a diagnostic test
(With real US data from the spring of 2020.) We have an antibody test for COVID-19. If 1000 COVID-19 positive patients are tested, on average 840 of them get a true-positive result (sensitivity 84%). If 1000 non-infected people are tested, 5 get a false-positive result (specificity \(1 - 0.005 = 0.995\), or 99.5%). About 1% of the population has been exposed to the virus. If a random person tests positive, what is the probability that this person is infected?

the hypothesis space has two members: \(H_1\) — infected, \(H_2\) — not infected;
priors: \(P(H_1) = 0.01\), \(P(H_2) = 1 - P(H_1) = 0.99\);
likelihoods: \(P(+ \mid H_1) = 0.84\) (sensitivity), \(P(+ \mid H_2) = 0.005\) (1 − specificity).



Show code
Pr_H1 <- 0.01
Pr_H2 <- 1 - Pr_H1
L_H1  <- 0.84
L_H2  <- 0.005
(Pr_infected <- (Pr_H1 * L_H1) / (Pr_H1 * L_H1 + Pr_H2 * L_H2))


[1] 0.6292135


The odds form makes the same calculation transparent. The prior odds of infection are \(0.01 / 0.99 \approx 1\!:\!99\). The likelihood ratio of a positive test — the diagnostic likelihood ratio — is sensitivity over one-minus-specificity:


Show code
prior_odds <- Pr_H1 / Pr_H2
LR_pos     <- L_H1 / L_H2          # = 0.84 / 0.005
post_odds  <- prior_odds * LR_pos
c(LR = LR_pos, weight_of_evidence_bans = log10(LR_pos),
  posterior_odds = post_odds,
  posterior_prob = post_odds / (1 + post_odds))


                     LR weight_of_evidence_bans          posterior_odds 
            168.0000000               2.2253093               1.6969697 
         posterior_prob 
              0.6292135 


A positive result carries a likelihood ratio of 168 — strong evidence, a little over two bans. Yet because the prior odds are so low (the disease is rare), the posterior probability of infection is only about 0.63: the strong evidence multiplies a small prior. This is the base-rate point of Chapter 2, now quantified.
There is a more intuitive route to the same number. Imagine 1000 random persons, 10 of whom are infected and 990 not. Of the infected, \(10 \times 0.84 = 8.4\) test positive; of the uninfected, \(990 \times 0.005 = 5\) test positive. The probability of being infected given a positive test is then \(8.4 / (8.4 + 5) = 0.63\).






The Infectious Diseases Society of America, in guidance reported by the New York Times (24 August 2020), made the practical version of this point: with a low base rate, antibody tests “should be used only for population surveys, not for diagnosing illness in individuals”, and only tests “correctly positive more than 96 percent of [the] time and correctly negative at least 99.5 percent of the time should be used”. A rare condition demands a very high likelihood ratio before a positive result means much for an individual.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
section: 9.6 A worked example: Madame Marie and the hypothesis space
text:
9.6 A worked example: Madame Marie and the hypothesis space
Chapter 7 introduced the hypothesis space and showed, with a trick coin, that the same data can support opposite headline conclusions in different spaces. This example develops that point with the full odds-form machinery, on a question with a longer pedigree.
Suppose we want to find out whether Madame Marie has extra-sensory perception (ESP). We use a deck of cards bearing one of five symbols, so that pure guessing succeeds with probability \(0.2\), and we record her guesses on \(n = 100\) cards. She gets \(k = 30\) correct — well above the 20 expected by chance.
A frequentist analysis compares this with the hypothesis of pure guessing alone and reports a small p-value: 30 or more correct is unlikely if she were guessing at random.


Show code
n <- 100; k <- 30
p_value <- pbinom(k - 1, n, 0.2, lower.tail = FALSE)  # P(X >= 30 | random)
p_value


[1] 0.01124898


The data are indeed inconsistent with pure randomness. But “inconsistent with randomness” is not “evidence for ESP”, because the p-value addresses only one hypothesis. Bayes’ theorem forces us to name the alternatives and their likelihoods. Consider three:

\(H_1\) — ESP: she perceives the card, raising her hit rate to, say, \(0.30\);
\(H_2\) — random guessing: hit rate \(0.20\);
\(H_3\) — bias: subtle cues, marked cards, or fraud also raise her hit rate to about \(0.30\).

The likelihoods are binomial (Chapter 6), and the two analyses — the naive two-hypothesis space \(\{H_1, H_2\}\) and the fuller \(\{H_1, H_2, H_3\}\) — differ only in which hypotheses are admitted and what priors they carry:


Show code
L1 <- dbinom(k, n, 0.30)   # ESP
L2 <- dbinom(k, n, 0.20)   # random
L3 <- dbinom(k, n, 0.30)   # bias: same hit rate as ESP

## Naive two-hypothesis space, generously agnostic between ESP and chance
prior2 <- c(ESP = 0.5, random = 0.5)
post2  <- prior2 * c(L1, L2)
post2  <- post2 / sum(post2)

## Fuller space: ESP a priori near-impossible; bias as plausible as chance
prior3 <- c(ESP = 1e-6, random = 0.5, bias = 0.5 - 1e-6)
post3  <- prior3 * c(L1, L2, L3)
post3  <- post3 / sum(post3)

list(LR_ESP_vs_random = L1 / L2,
     LR_ESP_vs_bias   = L1 / L3,
     posterior_2hyp   = round(post2, 4),
     posterior_3hyp_ESP = signif(post3["ESP"], 3))


$LR_ESP_vs_random
[1] 16.72251

$LR_ESP_vs_bias
[1] 1

$posterior_2hyp
   ESP random 
0.9436 0.0564 

$posterior_3hyp_ESP
     ESP 
1.89e-06 


Two things stand out. First, the likelihood ratio of ESP against random guessing is large, so in the naive two-hypothesis space the posterior probability of ESP comes out high — about 0.94 — the same impression the small p-value gives. Second, the likelihood ratio of ESP against bias is exactly 1: the data fit fraud precisely as well as they fit ESP, and so provide no evidence whatever to choose between them. Once \(H_3\) is admitted — and bias is, a priori, vastly more plausible than ESP — the posterior probability of ESP collapses to about \(10^{-6}\), unchanged from its prior. The data never bore on the question that matters.
The same data, the same likelihoods for ESP, two opposite conclusions: the difference is entirely in how the hypothesis space was sliced. This is the practical lesson. A p-value, comparing the data with a single null, can reject “pure randomness” while saying nothing about ESP versus bias — which is the comparison a scientist actually cares about. Evidence is comparative, and a relevant hypothesis left out of the space can invalidate the whole inference.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.7 Many hypotheses, and continuous parameters
More generally, for a sample space with \(n\) mutually exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses \(\Omega = \{H_1, H_2, \dots, H_n\}\),
\[P(d) = P(H_1)P(d\vert H_1) + P(H_2)P(d\vert H_2) + \dots + P(H_n)P(d\vert H_n).\]
This is the formula for total (a.k.a. marginal) probability, and Bayes’ theorem becomes
\[P(H_1\vert d) =\frac{P(H_1)P(d\vert H_1)}{P(H_1)P(d\vert H_1) + P(H_2)P(d \vert H_2) + \dots + P(H_n)P(d \vert H_n)}.\]
What if we want to estimate the true value of a continuous parameter (the probability that a patient dies of COVID-19, say, or the mean length of hospitalisation)? Then the hypothesis space has infinitely many members (the real numbers from 0 to 1, or the integers from 0 to infinity). We would need to specify infinitely many likelihoods and infinitely many priors before running the calculation. We can do this using continuous functions, which specify infinitely many points at once: prior and likelihood become probability distributions of the kind catalogued in Chapter 6, and the posterior is a continuous distribution too. The beta-binomial conjugacy of Chapter 6 is the cleanest case — a \(\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) prior and binomial data give a \(\text{Beta}(\alpha+s,\beta+f)\) posterior, with no integral to compute. When no such shortcut exists, the posterior is obtained numerically; the grid approximation of Chapter 9 is the most direct method, and Markov chain Monte Carlo (the appendix on MCMC) is the general one.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
section: 9.8 Updating, exchangeability, and what Bayes does not guarantee
text:
9.8 Updating, exchangeability, and what Bayes does not guarantee
Bayes’ theorem combines, in the logically optimal way, the evidence in the data (through the likelihood) with the data-independent beliefs (through the prior), and returns a posterior. There is no magic involved, just probability theory. Bayes’ theorem is not a truth machine — it combines the information put into it. If the prior or the likelihood is grossly wrong, there is no guarantee that the posterior converges on the truth, even in the long run (although under most realistic conditions it does).
Two practical properties follow. First, the theorem works iteratively, with no lower limit on the data: \(N = 1\) is fine.2 Yesterday’s posterior becomes today’s prior, new data enter as a new likelihood, and the updated posterior in turn becomes tomorrow’s prior. Bayesian inference thereby recapitulates the piecemeal nature of scientific inference, and because evidence is additive on the log scale (the weight-of-evidence section), accumulating studies is just addition. Second, there are no stopping rules: you may compute the posterior after each new observation without penalty.3 Because Bayesians compute the probabilities of hypotheses directly, they do not need the sampling distribution of the data, and so are not committed to a hypothetical infinite population of repetitions. Where frequentist statistics needs its data to be independent and identically distributed (iid; independence was defined in Chapter 5), Bayesian analysis needs only the weaker condition of exchangeability: the order in which the data points are processed must not affect the result.

Bayesian inference comes straight from probability theory; frequentist inference is a collection of procedures that require more stringent conditions to work properly.
crumbs: Part II. Probability is the logic of science
9  Bayes' theorem and the weight of evidence

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.9 Key points

Bayes’ theorem combines prior and likelihood into a posterior: \(P(H\vert d) \propto P(H)\,P(d\vert H)\). The denominator \(P(d)\) only normalises.
In odds form, posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. The \(P(d)\) cancels, separating the inference into what was known before (prior odds) and what the data contribute (the likelihood ratio, a.k.a. the Bayes factor for simple hypotheses).
The weight of evidence is the logarithm of the likelihood ratio; on the log scale Bayes’ theorem is additive, so independent studies sum.
Evidence is comparative: a likelihood addresses a hypothesis only relative to a named alternative. A likelihood ratio of 1 is no evidence, whatever the p-value says.
A rare condition (low prior) needs a large likelihood ratio before a positive test means much — the base-rate point, quantified (the diagnostic example).
How the hypothesis space is sliced determines the conclusion. A p-value compares the data with a single null and is silent on the comparison that matters; omitting a plausible hypothesis (bias, in the ESP example) can invalidate the inference.
Bayes’ theorem updates iteratively with no minimum \(N\) and no stopping rules, and requires only exchangeability, not iid. It is not a truth machine: rubbish in, rubbish out.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.10 Exercises

Odds form by hand. Repeat the diagnostic-test calculation for a population where the base rate is 10% rather than 1%, keeping the same sensitivity and specificity. Compute the posterior probability of infection both ways (direct Bayes and odds form), and report the weight of evidence of a positive test in bans. Why does the posterior change even though the likelihood ratio does not?
Evidence adds up. A patient takes the antibody test twice, independently, and both results are positive. Using the weight-of- evidence formula, add the two weights and convert back to a posterior probability (start from the 1% prior). Confirm the result by applying Bayes’ theorem twice, using the first posterior as the second prior.
Re-slice the deck. In the Madame Marie code, change Marie’s score to \(k = 45\) and re-run both analyses. Does the larger likelihood ratio against randomness change the three-hypothesis conclusion about ESP? Explain why or why not in terms of the likelihood ratio of ESP against bias.
Make bias implausible. Suppose the experiment is run under conditions that make fraud and cueing nearly impossible, so that the prior on \(H_3\) falls to \(10^{-4}\) while the prior on ESP stays at \(10^{-6}\). Recompute the three-hypothesis posterior for ESP. What does this tell you about where the real work of an ESP experiment lies — in the data or in the design?
From the cohort. Source R/simulate_cohort.R and generate the cohort. Estimate the stroke risk among treated and untreated patients, \(P(\text{stroke}\mid\text{drug})\) and \(P(\text{stroke}\mid\lnot\text{drug})\), by counting. Treat these as likelihoods and take a prior of 0.5 that a randomly chosen patient was treated; update on “this patient had a stroke” to obtain \(P(\text{drug}\mid\text{stroke})\). Explain why this posterior is an associational quantity and must not be read as the effect of the drug (Chapters 4 and 10).
Conceptual: the single null. A colleague reports “p = 0.001, so the effect is real.” Using the odds form and the ESP example, explain in a short paragraph what is missing from this inference and what additional quantities would be needed to make it.

Frequentist statistics does not work like this; there you need some minimum \(N\) for the algorithms to behave as advertised.↩︎
In frequentist statistics you need stopping rules (a predetermined sample size), so that you do not declare a “significant effect” the first time a randomly fluctuating p-value dips below the significance level. Bayesian inference has no significance level and no dichotomisation of continuous evidence, so stopping rules would be meaningless.↩︎

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.1 Fitting the binomial data model
Mortality of a disease is 50% and we have 3 patients. How many of them are likely to die? We have 2 pieces of data (mortality rate p = 0.5 and N = 3) and a 4-member sample space (0 dead, 1 dead, 2 dead, and 3 dead). We start by enumerating all logically possible scenarios (d - dead, a - alive)
If P(dead) = 0.5, then by simple counting we get that:
Thus we have 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8 possible futures that divide between the 4 hypotheses. This means that for each member of the parameter space we know the probability of its realization (P(1 death) = 3/8, etc.). It is this knowledge we now turn into a likelihood function.
Show code
# Parameter space: all possible futures
x <- seq(from = 0, to = 3)

# Likelihoods for each x value, 
# or P(deaths I x)
y <- c(1, 3, 3, 1)

ggplot(data=NULL, aes(x, y))+ 
  
  geom_point()+ 
  geom_line()+
  
  xlab("hypothetical nr of deaths")+ 
  
  ylab("plausibility")+ 
  theme_bw()
One death and two deaths are equilikely and one death is three times as likely as no deaths (or three deaths). Likelihood simply tells for each number of deaths, how likely is this outcome, given the mortality figure that we state.
Now we demonstrate the same using the binomial distribution model. The only difference is that now we get on the y-axis normalised probabilities.
Show code
y <- dbinom(x, 3, 0.5)

ggplot(data=NULL, aes(x, y)) + 
  
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+
  
  xlab("hypothetical nr of deaths")+ 
  
  ylab("probability")+ 
  theme_bw()
How many dead when we have 9 patients and mortality rate is 67 percent?
Show code
x <- seq(from = 0, to = 9)
y <- dbinom(x, 9, 0.67)

ggplot(data=NULL, aes(x, y)) + 
  
  geom_point()+
  
  geom_line()+
  
  xlab("hypothetical nr of deaths")+ 
  
  ylab("probability")+ 
  
  ggthemes::theme_tufte()
Next we add to the likelihood a flat prior and use the Bayes theorem.
Show code
x <- seq(from = 0 , to = 9) #parameter space: nr of deaths
prior <- rep(1 , 10) # flat prior

# Compute likelihood at each value in grid
likelihood <- dbinom(x, size = 9, prob = 0.67)

# Compute product of likelihood and prior
unstd.posterior <- likelihood * prior

# Normalise the posterior, so that it sums to 1
posterior <- unstd.posterior / sum(unstd.posterior)

ggplot(data = NULL, aes(x, posterior)) + 
  
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  
  xlab("hypothetical nr of deaths") + 
  
  ylab("posterior probability")+ 
  theme_bw()
Now its time for a shift of perspective. We want to estimate the true mortality rate.
We can still use binomial likelihood. dbinom() has 3 arguments, nr of events, nr of tries and probability of events. Again, we have two of them as data and one as the parameter whose value we want to estimate. We use the flat prior again. As there are Inf number of members in \(\Omega\), we cheat a little and calculate for the grid of 20 evenly spaced parameter values.
Show code
# grid: mortality at 20 evenly spaced probabilities from 0 to 1
x <- seq(from = 0 , to = 1, length.out = 20)

# prior
prior <- rep(1 , 20)

# likelihood at each value in grid
likelihood <- dbinom(6, size = 9 , prob = x)

posterior <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)

a <- tibble(x=rep(x=x, 2),
            
            y= c(likelihood, posterior),
            
            legend= rep(c("likelihood", "posterior"), each=20))

ggplot(data=a) + 
  
  geom_line(aes(x, y, color=legend))+ 
  
  ggthemes::theme_tufte()
Our posterior sums to 1, but thanks to flat prior its shape is the same as the likelihood.
Lets do this datapoint-by datapoint, so that n = 1.
First datapoint is that the 1st patient died.
Show code
likelihood <- dbinom(1, size = 1, prob = x)
posterior <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)
ggplot(data=NULL)+
  
  geom_line(aes(x, posterior), color= "blue")+ 
  
  ggthemes::theme_tufte()
Zero mortality is now logically impossible and 100 percent mortality is the hypothesis best supported by the data.
Second datapoint is that the 2nd patient died. Our previous posterior is now the prior.
Show code
prior <- posterior
likelihood <- dbinom(1 , size = 1, prob = x)
posterior1 <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)
ggplot(data=NULL)+
  
  geom_line(aes(x, prior))+
  
  geom_line(aes(x, posterior1), color="blue")+ 
  
  ggthemes::theme_tufte()
The posterior is no longer a straight line. 100 percent mortality is still the most likely mortality estimate.
Third datapoint is that the 3d patient survived.
Show code
prior <- posterior1
likelihood <- dbinom(0, size = 1, prob = x)
posterior2 <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)

ggplot(data=NULL)+
  
  geom_line(aes(x, prior))+
  
  geom_line(aes(x, posterior2), color="blue")+ 
  
  ggthemes::theme_tufte()
Now zero mortality and 100 percent mortality are both logically impossible. The most likely value for mortality is 2/3 or 75 percent.

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.2 The normal data model
Richard McElreath:

There are an infinite number of possible Gaussian distributions. Some have small means. Others have large means. Some are wide, with a large \(\sigma\). Others are narrow. We want our Bayesian machine to consider every possible distribution, each defined by a combination of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), and rank them by posterior plausibility. Posterior plausibility provides a measure of the logical compatibility of each possible distribution with the data and model. … The parameters to be estimated are both \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), so we need a prior \(Pr(\mu , \sigma)\), the joint prior probability for all parameters. In most cases, priors are specified independently for each parameter, which amounts to assuming \(Pr(\mu, \sigma) = Pr(\mu) Pr(\sigma)\).

How does one make a US president? Lets start by generating some heights of presidential candidates. We assume that human growth is a deterministic process that depends on a complex mix of many genetic and environmental factors. But we really do not understand this process well enough to directly use it to generate prospective heights of future presidents. We think that human height is approximately normally distributed (conditional on sex, age, etc.), so we could model presidential heights as a normal distribution where each possible height is given a probability of occurring. Now, we could generate new heights from this stochastic model proportionally to these probabilities. But before we do this, we have to fix the shape of the normal distribution so that we know the relevant probabilities. This can be done by fixing the values of two parameters of the normal distribution, \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). Luckily we have data on the heights of the last 12 presidents:


Show code
heights <- tibble(value = c(183, 192, 182, 183, 177, 185, 188, 188, 182, 185, 188, 182))


As the parameter \(\mu\) is identical to the expected value, i.e. the mean of the normal distribution and \(\sigma\) to standard deviation (SD), we can simply calculate those and then use these numbers to generate new heights.
Data mean is:


Show code
(Mean <- mean(heights$value))


[1] 184.5833


and SD is:


Show code
(SD <- sd(heights$value))


[1] 3.964807


Predict 4000 new heights and calculate standard deviation:


Show code
set.seed(1)
rnorm(4000, Mean, SD) %>% sd()


[1] 4.10711


This procedure is not ideal, though, as it does not take into account the fact that our estimates of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), calculated from limited data, are not precisely true for the full population of US presidents, including the future ones. So on top of the randomness in predicting new presidents that comes from our imperfect knowledge of the mechanisms that generate human heights we must model the uncertainty that comes from imperfect data. How can we do this? When modelling this 2nd order epistemic uncertainty we will to end up not with point estimates of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), but probability distributions for \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) values. This way we are not predicting new heights from a single fixed normal distribution, but rather from many different distributions, where each is parametrised by a plausible combination of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) values (each of these combinations is supported by the data and by our prior knowledge of plausible presidential heights).


Show code
pres_m <- brm(data = heights, formula = value~1, file="models/pres_m")
pres_posterior_sample <- posterior_samples(pres_m)
set.seed(1)
rnorm(4000, pres_posterior_sample$b_Intercept, pres_posterior_sample$sigma) %>% sd()


[1] 4.546833


Now the standard deviation of predicted presidents heights is slightly larger (by 0.44 cm), reflecting the extra uncertainty. Note that the model pools both kinds of uncertainties so that we cannot re-separate them in later analysis.
Next we fit this model the old-fashioned way, using the Bayes theorem with grid approximation.
Basic Bayesian inference goes like this:

What is the sample space of true mean heights? From -Inf to Inf. Silly, but convenient, if we want to use the normal data model (likelihood).
How likely it is for each possible height to be the true average? The answer to this question is the likelihood, which depends on our sample data and on the model we choose to represent this data with. Here we model the likelihood as a normal distribution, whose mean equals the sample mean and whose standard deviation equals the sample sd/sqrt(N), or SEM (standard error of the mean).
Next step is quantifying prior beliefs, independent of sample data, about the mean height. Our prior for the mean is also normal distribution with \(\mu = 175.4\) (the mean height of US males), sd = 3 (picked so, that a mean height of 181 cm for the presidents would still be fairly possible). And the prior for \(\sigma\) is also normal with \(\mu = 5.2\) (the SD for the heights of the general US male population) and sd=1 (so that true SD values between about 3 and 7 cm would be possible enough). This is a rather informative prior.
Then we calculate the posterior.2

Some preliminary points:

Likelihood models data as a probability distribution.
Likelihood does not have to be normal.
Prior is your belief about the parameter value, modelled as a probability distribution.
Prior does not have to be normal.
Likelihood and prior(s) do not have to be represented by the same distribution.
Posterior is narrower than prior and likelihood. This reflects the combining of information in the likelihood and prior. Bayes theorem is provably the most efficient way of doing this.

Now, lets go on. Next item in the menu is the grid method for posterior in 2D. Instead of multiplying likelihoods, we will add log-likelihoods (which is mathematically the same thing).
The model is:
\[height_i \sim normal(\mu, \sigma)\]
\[\mu \sim normal(175.4, 5)\]
\[\sigma \sim normal(5.2, 1)\]
Where the 1. line is the likelihood, containing two parameters, and the next 2 lines are priors for each parameter.
i is index for heights, which means that the model assumes that each individual height comes from the same normal distribution.

10.2.1 prior predictive simulation
Here we calculate the posterior solely on the prior. As we add no likelihood, the data has no influence on the posterior – only the prior does.


Show code
mu_prior1 <- rnorm(10000, 175.4, 5)
mu_prior2 <- rnorm(10000, 180, 50)

sigma_prior1 <- rnorm(10000, 5.2, 1)
sigma_prior2 <- runif(10000, 0, 100)

y1 <- rnorm(10000, mu_prior1, sigma_prior1)
y2 <- rnorm(10000, mu_prior2, sigma_prior2)

ggplot(data=NULL, aes(x=y1)) + 
  geom_density()+ 
  
  geom_density(aes(x=y2), color="red")+
  
  xlab("mean presidents height")+ theme_bw()





A prior predictive check.




We use two different prior combinations: one is informative (the black line in the figure) and another one is weakly informative (red), meaning that it carries no useful biological information, but nevertheless gives a lot more weight to positive values and values < 4 meters (that’s right - this prior assumes that 4-meter mean height is possible). Currently, weak priors are all the rage, because they make model fitting by MCMC methods easier, while requiring minimal scientific input. Lets hope that this situation is about to change in favour of strong scientifically informed priors!


10.2.2 Calculating the 2D posterior
The posterior is a joint distribution over all parameters in the model. If we have 2 parameters, then we have a 2D posterior. If we have 200 parameters, then we have 200D posterior. We can always collapse the posterior to a desired 1D view for inspection (see below).


Show code
# d_grid contains all possible combinations (10 000) of mu and sigma values. 
n <- 100
d_grid <- crossing(mu = seq(from = 180, to = 190, length.out = n),

#crossing() expands the table to cover all possible combinations.
                  
                   sigma = seq(from = 1, to = 8, length.out = n))

#grid_function generates a density value from a normal function, 
#whose x is a vector of presidents height and mu and sigma are plucked from d_grid.
#sum() in the log-scale is prod() in the linear scale. In each row of d_grid 
#we multiply likelihoods (actually, sum log-likelihoods) for each data point, using
#different combinations of mu and sigma to model the normal distribution.

grid_function <- function(mu, sigma) {
  
  dnorm(heights$value, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE) %>% sum()
  
}


d_grid <- d_grid %>% 
  
  mutate(log_likelihood = map2_dbl(mu, sigma, grid_function),
    
# map2_dbl() takes each mu and sigma pair in d_grid (row-wise) and puts it into the grid_function
         
         prior_mu    = dnorm(mu, mean = 175.4, sd  = 5, log = TRUE),
         
#for each value of mu (one in each row) we calculate normal density from prior distr.
         
         prior_sigma = dnorm(sigma, mean = 5.2, sd = 1, log = TRUE),

#for each value of sigma we calculate normal density from prior distr. for sigma
         
         product = log_likelihood + prior_mu + prior_sigma,
         
#sum() in the log-scale is product in the linear scale. 

         probability = exp(product - max(product)))
#product - max(product) mirrors into negative scale, which after exp() becomes probability scale.
#probability vector contains the posterior probabilities across mu and sigma. 

d_grid %>% ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = sigma, z = probability)) + 
  
  geom_contour() + theme_classic()









This 2D posterior is drawn as a 3D surface, where the third dimension is posterior probability. 3 In the centre of the contour is the peak of the posterior distribution. This is, by the way, a bivariate normal distribution.


10.2.3 Sampling from the posterior – 1D posteriors for mu and sigma.
I am sampling randomly while weighting on probability, so that mu values with higher posterior probability are more likely to end up in the sample. From such random samples of mu and sigma (the posterior samples) we can plot the posteriors:


Show code
d_grid_samples <- 
  d_grid %>% 
  sample_n(size = 1e4, replace = TRUE, weight = probability)

d_grid_samples %>% 
  
  pivot_longer(mu:sigma) %>% 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) + 
  
  geom_density() +
  
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free")











10.2.4 summarising the posterior (95% HDI)


Show code
posterior_summary(d_grid_samples[,1:2])


        Estimate Est.Error      Q2.5      Q97.5
mu    183.951485 1.3195671 181.31313 186.565657
sigma   4.755323 0.7611191   3.40404   6.373737




10.2.5 Triplot for mu


Show code
prior_mu <-  rnorm(10000, mean = 175.4, sd  = 5)
lik_mu <- rnorm(10000, mean= mean(heights$value), 
                sd = sd(heights$value)/sqrt( nrow(heights) ) )
post_mu <- d_grid_samples$mu

ggplot(data=NULL, aes(prior_mu)) + 
  
  geom_density() +
  
  geom_density(aes(lik_mu), color="firebrick") +
  
  geom_density(aes(post_mu), color="navyblue") +
  
  xlab("Mean presidents height")+
  
  ggtitle("prior (black), likelihood(red), \nand posterior (blue)")+
  
  theme_classic()









Even with only 12 datapoints the prior is so much wider than likelihood that it has minimal influence on the posterior.


10.2.6 Some things to notice

As the priors are true probabilities that sum to one, and the likelihoods are not, we can run our models on either priors and data, or on priors alone, but never on data alone. Running a model on priors alone can be a good idea, if you want to know, how much your data influences the model fit. When you have little data and strong priors, this is the thing to do.
Each fitted model with k parameters gives you a k-dimensional posterior (this is slightly more complicated with multi-level models), which we flatten into k side-by-side variables in the posterior samples table. This means that we have to treat each row of this table as a single unit, when we use them in further calculations. In each row there is one plausible combination of k parameter values – if you mix the values between rows, this might no longer hold.4
As we fitted the full model (both mean and sd), we can generate in silico data from it, using the full posterior samples, and compare these generated data with the actual data that was used to fit the model. By this we mean that all Bayesian models are generative. This comparison is called a posterior predictive check and it is a very convenient method to get a first impression on how well your mathematical model recaptures the physical data generating mechanism in the nature. PP check is a major advantage of Bayesian modelling, as the usual frequentist models that estimate the mean, do not estimate the sd. Such frequentist models are not generative.
The more data you have, the narrower the likelihood; the more scientific information you put into the prior, the narrower the prior (usually, but not always). Whichever of the two is narrower, will influence the posterior more. The posterior will always be narrower than likelihood and prior. A lot of data swamps the prior, making it unimportant in respect of the posterior. Conversely, with a small sample the prior can have a major influence on the posterior.
In Bayesian estimation, posterior is everything. It contains all of the information about the estimates that is contained in the fitted model. There is nothing in the model about the parameter values that is not covered in the posterior. Every fitted model gives you a posterior for every parameter in the model. This is it. All you have to do, is to study those posteriors, and to make calculations with them to get new estimates. For example, we will soon learn, how to get the estimate for a group mean by adding another group mean and the effect size. These calculations are done at the level of posterior samples, the idea being that you do not want to lose information about estimation uncertainty. Also, with many likelihoods you can calculate straight from the posterior either the mean or the median (and often the mode), all with appropriate credible intervals. This is not something you can easily do in frequentist statistics.
