title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.3 Bridge to regression
Everything in this chapter generalises. A regression model is a data model whose parameter — the mean of the likelihood — is itself a function of predictors: \(\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\) instead of a single \(\mu\). The president-height model above is already the simplest regression, an intercept-only normal model (value ~ 1); adding predictors on the right-hand side is the whole of Part V. The machinery does not change — prior × likelihood, normalised, summarised by samples and a credible interval — only the number of parameters grows, and with it the need to replace the grid with MCMC (the appendix on MCMC). Chapter 20 takes up linear regression, Chapter 24 the generalised linear models whose exponential-family likelihoods were previewed in Chapter 6, and Chapter 28 returns the posterior samples to causal use, turning a fitted model into a distribution of counterfactual contrasts.

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.4 Key points

Grid approximation is Bayes’ theorem applied directly: evaluate prior × likelihood over a grid of parameter values and normalise so the posterior sums to one. It makes every step of Chapter 8 visible.
The likelihood models the data as a probability distribution and need not be normal; the prior models data-independent belief and need not match the likelihood’s form. The posterior is narrower than either, because it combines their information.
Updating one datapoint at a time gives the same posterior as updating all at once (exchangeability, Chapter 8): yesterday’s posterior is today’s prior.
Prior predictive simulation draws parameters from the prior and then data from the model, revealing what a prior implies before the data — a weakly informative prior can imply absurd values (4-metre presidents).
The posterior over \(k\) parameters is \(k\)-dimensional; collapse it to one parameter by sampling and reading off a marginal. Treat each posterior sample (a full row of parameter values) as a unit when computing derived quantities.
Summarise a posterior by a point (mean, median, or mode) and a credible interval — the 95% HDI is the narrowest interval holding 95% of the posterior mass, and unlike a confidence interval it means what students expect: the parameter lies in it with 95% probability.
The posterior is everything the fitted model says about the parameters; further estimates are calculations on posterior samples. Because Bayesian models are generative, the same samples support posterior predictive checks.
More data narrows the likelihood; more informative priors narrow the prior; the narrower one dominates, and a large sample swamps the prior.

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.5 Exercises

Grid on the cohort. Source R/simulate_cohort.R, take the untreated patients, and estimate the stroke risk by grid approximation: a grid of 200 probabilities, a flat prior, and a binomial likelihood with the observed stroke count and number of patients. Plot the posterior, report its mean and 95% HDI, and compare the mean with the raw proportion. Then replace the flat prior with a \(\text{Beta}(2,2)\)-shaped prior evaluated on the grid and describe how the posterior moves.
Order does not matter. Re-run the datapoint-by-datapoint update of the three patients (died, died, survived) in a different order (e.g. survived, died, died). Confirm the final posterior is identical, and explain which property from Chapter 8 guarantees this.
A reckless prior. In the prior predictive chunk, replace the informative height prior with \(\mu \sim \text{Normal}(180, 50)\), \(\sigma \sim \text{Uniform}(0,100)\) and plot the implied heights. What fraction of simulated mean heights are negative or above 3 metres? Use this to argue, in two sentences, for scientifically informed priors.
HDI versus equal-tailed interval. From the posterior samples of \(\mu\), compute both the 95% HDI and the 2.5%–97.5% quantile interval. For this near-symmetric posterior they nearly coincide; sketch (in words) a skewed posterior for which they would differ, and say which interval you would report.
The posterior is everything. Using the posterior samples of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), estimate the probability that a newly drawn president exceeds 190 cm (draw one height per posterior sample with rnorm and take the proportion). Explain why this calculation must be done row-wise on the samples rather than by plugging in the posterior means.
Why the grid runs out. Re-run the binomial grid with 20, 200, and 2000 points and note when the posterior summaries stop changing. Then explain why the same brute-force grid is infeasible for a model with 30 parameters, and what replaces it (the appendix on MCMC).

While multiple testing, narrowly understood, is not a problem for the Bayesian, false alarms are. The currently favoured Bayesian mitigation of false alarms is multilevel modelling.↩︎
This is Bayesian method in a nutshell: at each parameter value (x) we multiply the likelihood (y_lik) with the prior (y_pr), thus combining our prior knowledge with the data and the data model. Knowledge (prior and data) in – knowledge (posterior) out.↩︎
geom_contour() visualizes 3D surfaces in 2D. To specify a valid surface, the data must contain x, y, and z coordinates, and each unique combination of x and y can appear once.↩︎
With the normal likelihood it will actually hold, because the variation of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are independent of each other, but this is not so with most other likelihoods.↩︎

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
text:
11.1 A second outcome that never happens
Fix a patient and a binary treatment — our blood-pressure drug, \(A = 1\) for treated, \(A = 0\) for not. Write \(Y(1)\) for the stroke outcome this patient would have under treatment and \(Y(0)\) for the outcome the same patient would have without it. These hypotheticals are the potential outcomes: two values attached to one person, only one of which the world will ever reveal. The patient’s individual causal effect is the contrast \(Y(1) - Y(0)\) — which is, in general, unknowable, because we see the patient under one treatment only. The other potential outcome is a counterfactual: real enough to define, impossible to observe. This is Holland’s fundamental problem of causal inference.
Two assumptions glue this notation to data. The first is consistency: the outcome we actually observe is the potential outcome for the treatment actually received, \(Y = Y(A)\). It sounds trivial, but is not — it presumes the intervention is well defined, that “treated” refers to one thing and not to a bundle of different things with different effects (the dose, route, adherence). The second is no interference (part of SUTVA): one patient’s treatment does not change another’s outcome, so \(Y_i(a)\) depends on patient \(i\)’s own treatment alone. Both can fail — interference is the rule in vaccine and network studies — and when they do, the contrast \(Y(1)-Y(0)\) is no longer the right target and has to be redefined; how depends on which part broke (see below).
In real life the counterfactual column is missing. In our simulated cohort it is not: we could compute each patient’s risk under both treatments. It is worth looking at the thing we almost never get to see.
Show code
df <- simulate_cohort(n = 10000, seed = 2024)

cohort <- as_tibble(df) |>                            # the observable cohort, plus ...
  bind_cols(as_tibble(attr(df, "oracle")) |>          # ... the oracle's potential-outcome
              select(risk0, risk1))                   #     risks Y(0) and Y(1)

cohort |>
  filter(id %in% 1:6) |>
  transmute(id, severity = round(severity, 1), drug, observed_stroke = stroke,
            `risk Y(0)` = risk0, `risk Y(1)` = risk1, `risk difference` = risk1 - risk0) |>

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
text:
SUTVA: what lets us write \(Y_i(a)\) at all



The notation \(Y_i(a)\) — one potential outcome per unit per treatment level — comes from the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA, Rubin’s term). It has two parts, both of which must hold for the expression even to make sense.

No interference. Unit \(i\)’s potential outcomes depend only on \(i\)’s own treatment, so we may write \(Y_i(a)\) rather than \(Y_i(a_1, a_2, \dots)\). This fails whenever one unit’s treatment can influence another — vaccines and herd immunity, infectious disease, treated partners in a household, classroom- or village-level assignment, market-wide effects. Then each unit has a separate potential outcome for every configuration of everyone’s treatment, and the tidy contrast \(Y(1) - Y(0)\) is not even defined.
One version of treatment (no hidden variations). “Treated” must name a single, well-specified intervention. If \(A = 1\) secretly bundles many versions with different effects — different doses, formulations, surgeons, or simply different ways of “being treated” — then \(Y(1)\) is an average over an unspecified mixture and changes meaning with it. This is the same demand as consistency: \(Y = Y(A)\) is only informative when \(A = 1\) refers to one thing.

SUTVA is therefore not a box to tick at the end of an analysis; it is the licence to write the estimand in the first place. When meeting it is doubtful, one should sharpen the intervention (a specific dose and schedule) or model the interference explicitly (partial-interference or network designs), rather than press on with an ambiguous \(Y(a)\). It is also why an “effect” of a fixed attribute — the “effect of sex”, say, or “of race” — strains the framework: there is no agreed intervention that sets such a variable, so its potential outcome has no settled referent (contrast a modifiable trait like obesity, where the trouble is the opposite — many different ways one could intervene, with different effects). This is the well-defined-intervention point we return to at the end of the chapter.








How \(Y(1)-Y(0)\) is redefined depends on which half of SUTVA gave way



If the failure is interference, a unit’s outcome depends on the whole pattern of treatment, then the potential outcome gains arguments — \(Y_i(\mathbf{a})\), a function of the entire assignment vector \(\mathbf{a} = (a_1, \dots, a_n)\) rather than of \(a_i\) alone. That is up to \(2^n\) potential outcomes per person instead of two, which is hopeless without structure, so one must impose some. Partial interference assumes units sit in groups — households, classrooms, villages — with spillover only within a group; an exposure mapping assumes further that a unit’s outcome depends on the rest only through a low-dimensional summary, typically the coverage \(c\) (the fraction treated in its group), which collapses the outcome to \(Y_i(a_i, c)\) in own-treatment \(a_i\) and coverage \(c\). The single contrast then splits into a family of well-defined effects:

a direct effect — switch my own treatment, holding the group’s coverage fixed;
an indirect, or spillover, effect — change the group’s coverage, holding my own treatment fixed (the protection an unvaccinated person gains from a vaccinated community);
a total effect — the two together, treated-under-high-coverage versus untreated-under-low; and
an overall effect — compare two whole allocation programmes, say 0% against 70% coverage, averaged over everyone.

Which of these is “the” effect?: “should this patient be vaccinated?” asks for the direct effect; “should we fund a 70%-coverage programme?” asks for the overall effect; and — herd immunity being the point of vaccination — the two can diverge sharply. These effects are not mere definitions: once the exposure structure is recorded — who was treated directly, and who only through a treated network member — they are identifiable and routinely estimated in network-randomised trials with standard correlated-data methods.1
If instead the failure is multiple versions of treatment, redefinition means naming the version. The estimand becomes the effect of one specified intervention — a dose, a schedule, a surgical technique — or, when the versions genuinely cannot be pinned down, the effect of a stated distribution over them (a “modified treatment policy” that assigns versions as they arise in practice). Either way the manoeuvre is the same in spirit: replace a vague switch with a contrast of interventions sharp enough that \(Y(\cdot)\) has a single value again — which is, in the end, the lesson of the well-defined-intervention caveat at the close of this chapter.

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
section: 11.2 The estimands: average effects and their scales
text:
11.2 The estimands: average effects and their scales
As individual effects are out of reach, we target averages. The average treatment effect is the contrast of potential outcomes over the whole population, \[ \text{ATE} \;=\; E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)], \] the stroke risk if everyone were treated against the risk if no one were. A close relative is the average treatment effect in the treated, \(\text{ATT} = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid A = 1]\), the effect among the patients who actually got the drug — a different and often more policy-relevant quantity whenever the effect varies across people. Its counterpart, the average treatment effect in the untreated, \(\text{ATU} = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid A = 0]\), asks what the drug would do for those who did not receive it. This is the estimand behind a decision to extend treatment to them, as against ATT’s question of whether to withdraw it from those who have it. The three are tied by the share treated, \(\text{ATE} = P(A{=}1)\,\text{ATT} + P(A{=}0)\,\text{ATU}\), so once the effect varies across people they part company — and the gap between ATT and ATU is itself a causal signal: it says whether treatment reached the people it helps most. These are estimands: precise targets chosen before estimation, not whatever a model happens to spit out.
A contrast also needs a scale, the choice of which is substantive. The same two risks \(E[Y(1)]\) and \(E[Y(0)]\) can be reported as a risk difference \(E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]\), a risk ratio \(E[Y(1)]/E[Y(0)]\), or an odds ratio. They answer different questions — absolute public-health burden versus relative effect — and they are not interchangeable; the odds ratio in particular is non-collapsible, so it can shift when you add covariates even with no confounding (Chapter 24). Our oracle reports all of them.






Odds ratios and hazard ratios make poor causal estimands



Of the scales above, the risk difference and risk ratio are collapsible and are on the probability scale a patient or policy-maker actually reasons in. The odds ratio and the hazard ratio are neither, and both should be avoided as causal summaries.
Non-collapsibility. A measure is collapsible when the population (marginal) value is a weighted average of the stratum-specific ones; the risk difference and risk ratio are, while the odds ratio is not. The consequence is unsettling: with no confounding whatsoever, the odds ratio adjusted for a covariate differs from the unadjusted one — adding a risk factor that only causally affects the outcome, but has no causal link to the treatment, to a logistic model does not bias the causal interpretation of RR and RD (while narrowing the CI-s), while it drives the OR away from 1. So the OR depends on which covariates are included in the model for reasons that have nothing to do with bias, two correctly specified analyses can report different ORs, and you cannot read a population-average effect off a logistic coefficient (Chapter 24). This is not confounding but it makes the OR treacherous to interpret and to compare across studies.
Under a logistic risk model the mechanism is explicit. If \(\operatorname{logit} P(Y{=}1 \mid A, L) = \alpha + \beta A + \gamma L\), then \(\beta\) is the log-odds-ratio within a level of \(L\) — a conditional effect. The marginal log-odds-ratio, obtained by averaging the fitted risks over the distribution of \(L\) and only then forming the odds ratio, is smaller in magnitude than \(\beta\) whenever \(\gamma \neq 0\), because the logit is nonlinear and the odds ratio of an average is not the average of the odds ratios. The gap is present even when \(L\) is independent of \(A\), so it is not confounding: the conditional and marginal odds ratios are distinct estimands, and adding a pure outcome predictor to the model increases the magnitude of \(\beta\) while leaving the marginal odds ratio unchanged. A logistic coefficient is therefore specific to its adjustment set and is not comparable across models that condition on different covariates. To obtain a marginal odds ratio from a logistic fit, average the predicted risks over the covariate distribution and form the contrast on the risk scale (standardisation, Chapter 12) rather than exponentiating \(\beta\).2
The hazard ratio is non-collapsible in the same way.
Odds (P/(1 - P)) are not probabilities (P). An odds ratio ((P1/(1 - P1))/(P2/(1 - P2)) approximates the risk ratio (P1/P2) only when the outcome is rare. For purely mathematical reasons, an OR always exaggerates the effect in comparison to RR; for a common outcome it exaggerates a lot: against a \(30\%\) baseline risk, an OR of \(2.0\) corresponds to a just \(46\%\) increase, and to a RR of about \(1.5\). People routinely misread an OR as an RR and so overstate the effect. Odds answer no question a clinician or a patient actually asks; risks do.
Hazard ratios hide a selection effect. A hazard at time \(t\) is a rate among those still event-free at \(t\). Once treatment has begun to act, the survivors in the two arms are no longer comparable — treatment has selectively kept some high-risk people event-free, so the treated risk set is frailer than the control risk set. The hazard ratio therefore conditions on a post-treatment variable (survival), blending the genuine effect with a time-varying depletion-of-susceptibles selection.3 That is why a constant hazard ratio need not reflect a constant individual effect, and why even a flawless randomised trial can report a hazard ratio with no clean causal interpretation. The proportional-hazards assumption that compresses HR to a single number rarely holds either.
What to report instead. Prefer estimands that are collapsible, on the probability scale, and tied to an intervention: the risk difference and risk ratio at a stated time horizon, survival or cumulative-incidence differences, or the restricted mean survival time. This book targets the ATE on the risk-difference and risk-ratio scales throughout.




Show code
estimands <- cohort |>
  summarise(
    crude_RD = mean(stroke[drug == 1]) - mean(stroke[drug == 0]),
    crude_RR = mean(stroke[drug == 1]) / mean(stroke[drug == 0]),
    ATE_RD   = mean(risk1) - mean(risk0),
    ATE_RR   = mean(risk1) / mean(risk0),
    ATE_OR   = (mean(risk1) / (1 - mean(risk1))) / (mean(risk0) / (1 - mean(risk0))),
    ATT_RD   = mean(risk1[drug == 1] - risk0[drug == 1]))

estimands |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "estimand", values_to = "value")


# A tibble: 6 x 2
  estimand   value
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 crude_RD  0.0186
2 crude_RR  1.57  
3 ATE_RD   -0.0268
4 ATE_RR    0.601 
5 ATE_OR    0.584 
6 ATT_RD   -0.0388


The true ATE is protective on every scale — a risk ratio of 0.6, about 2.7 strokes prevented per hundred treated. The crude contrast, the thing a naive analysis reports, says the opposite: a risk ratio of 1.57 — the drug looks harmful. Both numbers are computed from the same cohort. Only one is the effect.
The treated and the untreated are not given the same effect, and how they differ is worth a look. Compare the ATT and the ATU on both scales:


Show code
att_atu <- cohort |>
  group_by(drug) |>
  summarise(RD = mean(risk1 - risk0),                 # E[Y(1) - Y(0)] within the arm
            RR = mean(risk1) / mean(risk0), .groups = "drop")

att <- att_atu |> filter(drug == 1)                   # treated   -> ATT
atu <- att_atu |> filter(drug == 0)                   # untreated -> ATU

att_atu |>
  transmute(group = if_else(drug == 1, "treated (ATT)", "untreated (ATU)"), RD, RR)


# A tibble: 2 x 3
  group                RD    RR
  <chr>             <dbl> <dbl>
1 untreated (ATU) -0.0122 0.635
2 treated (ATT)   -0.0388 0.591


On the risk-difference scale the drug averts far more among the treated (ATT \(\approx\) -0.039) than it would among the untreated (ATU \(\approx\) -0.012) — nearly three times the absolute benefit. Yet on the risk-ratio scale the two are all but identical (0.591 versus 0.635). Both facts hold because the drug cuts risk by a near-constant fraction, and the treated are the sicker patients, with much higher baseline risk, so the same relative cut delivers a larger absolute reduction. The confounding-by-indication that ruins the crude comparison thus has a flip side — treatment was steered toward exactly those with the most absolute risk to lose. Whether “the effect” is larger in the treated is therefore not a fact about the drug but about the scale you read it on (Chapter 16). ATT, ATU and ATE coincide only when the effect is homogeneous on that scale. That the ratio scale is so often the one on which effects are near-homogeneous — genuine interaction being comparatively rare multiplicatively — is a broad empirical regularity;4 the catch is that a constant risk ratio forces a risk difference that climbs with baseline risk, so the more portable scale is not the one a public-health decision actually needs.
The absolute effect can be easier to grasp as a number needed to treat (NNT): the number of patients one must treat, to prevent a single event over a stated period. It is the reciprocal of the absolute risk difference, \(\text{NNT} = 1/|\text{RD}|\), so it carries the causal content of the RD. An NNT built from the ATE is a population causal quantity, while an NNT built from the crude risk difference is every bit as confounded as that difference. From the cohort’s true ATE, \(\text{NNT} \approx\) 38: treat about 40 patients to avert one stroke. In our example, the NNT is far smaller in the high-risk treated (NNT \(\approx\) 26) than in the lower-risk untreated (NNT \(\approx\) 82), even though the relative effect is identical in the two groups. An NNT is not a property of the drug alone but of the drug applied to a particular baseline risk over a particular time horizon, and it must be reported with both. Turned around, a harmful contrast yields a number needed to harm: taken at face value, this cohort’s crude comparison would pin an NNH of about 54 on a drug that in truth prevents strokes.

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
section: 11.3 Why the crude contrast is not the effect
text:
11.3 Why the crude contrast is not the effect
The crude contrast estimates the association \(E[Y \mid A=1] - E[Y \mid A=0]\), and an association is a comparison of different patients — those who took the drug versus those who did not. The causal effect is a comparison of the same patients across worlds. The gap between them has an exact algebraic form. Among the treated, what we observe is \(E[Y \mid A=1] = E[Y(1) \mid A=1]\) by consistency; among the untreated, \(E[Y \mid A=0] = E[Y(0) \mid A=0]\). Add and subtract the missing counterfactual \(E[Y(0) \mid A=1]\) — the risk the treated would have run untreated — and the association splits cleanly: \[
\underbrace{E[Y\mid A{=}1] - E[Y\mid A{=}0]}_{\text{association}}
=\underbrace{E[Y(1)\mid A{=}1]-E[Y(0)\mid A{=}1]}_{\text{ATT: a real effect}}
+\underbrace{E[Y(0)\mid A{=}1]-E[Y(0)\mid A{=}0]}_{\text{confounding bias}} .
\] The second term is the whole problem. It compares the untreated risk of the treated with the untreated risk of the untreated — two groups that, if treatment was assigned for a reason, were never alike to begin with. Normally it is invisible, because \(E[Y(0)\mid A=1]\) is counterfactual. The oracle shows it to us.


Show code
EY0 <- cohort |>
  group_by(drug) |>
  summarise(EY0 = mean(risk0), .groups = "drop")      # untreated risk E[Y(0)] in each arm

EY0_treated   <- EY0 |> filter(drug == 1) |> pull(EY0)   # E[Y(0) | A=1]  -- counterfactual
EY0_untreated <- EY0 |> filter(drug == 0) |> pull(EY0)   # E[Y(0) | A=0]  -- observable

tibble(`E[Y(0)|treated]`   = EY0_treated,
       `E[Y(0)|untreated]` = EY0_untreated,
       confounding_gap     = EY0_treated - EY0_untreated)


# A tibble: 1 x 3
  `E[Y(0)|treated]` `E[Y(0)|untreated]` confounding_gap
              <dbl>               <dbl>           <dbl>
1            0.0950              0.0335          0.0615


The treated, had they gone untreated, would have had a stroke risk of 0.095 — nearly three times the 0.034 of those actually untreated. The treated were sicker all along (the drug goes to high-severity patients), so the confounding term is large and positive, 0.061, and it swamps the genuinely protective ATT, turning a beneficial drug into an apparently harmful one. This is confounding by indication, seen for once with the counterfactual laid bare rather than inferred.

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
section: 11.4 What it takes to identify an effect
text:
11.4 What it takes to identify an effect
If the bias is the term \(E[Y(0)\mid A=1] - E[Y(0)\mid A=0]\), the cure is any condition that erases it.

Exchangeability. The treated and untreated groups are comparable: \(Y(a) \perp A\). In other words, if we had, contrafactually, given the treatment to the placebo group and vice versa, the causal estimate would not have changed. Marginally this is a strong demand, met by design in RCTs by randomisation (Chapter 4). In observational studies we aim for the weaker conditional exchangeability, \(Y(a) \perp A \mid L\): comparability within levels of a set of covariates \(L\). This means that for exchangeability we need to have the full adjustment set, measured correctly, and modelled correctly. The next chapter shows how to think of this with the help of graphs (DAGs).
Positivity. Every kind of patient could, with some non-zero probability, have received either treatment: \(0 < P(A = a \mid L) < 1\) for every \(L\) that occurs. Without it there are strata with no treated (or no untreated) patients to compare, and nonparametrically no amount of data fills the hole. Two kinds of failure are worth separating. A structural violation — some stratum can never be treated, a contraindication say — is a hole in the question itself, mendable only by restricting the target population or redefining the intervention. A practical violation is mere finite-sample sparsity, and how much it costs depends on the estimator: inverse-probability weighting is the most fragile, near-empty strata throwing up extreme weights and unstable estimates (Chapter 12), whereas an outcome model extrapolates across the gap — which rescues identification only by leaning on its functional form in a region the data barely constrain.5 Either way the assumption does not disappear; modelling merely trades a requirement on the data for a stronger one on the model.
Consistency. As above: the intervention is well defined and \(Y = Y(A)\). When “treated” is really a bundle of versions, what gets identified is the effect of the mixture of versions as it arose in this population — a quantity that need not carry over to a population where the mixture differs.6

When the above conditions hold, the counterfactual mean is identified — written entirely in terms of observable quantities: \[ E[Y(a)] \;=\; \sum_{l} E[Y \mid A=a,\, L=l]\; P(L=l). \] This is standardisation, and equivalently the g-formula: estimate the risk within each stratum of \(L\), then average over the population’s mix of \(L\). It is the whole of Chapter 12, and inverse-probability weighting is its mirror image. The formula also exposes the two assumptions: it needs every stratum to contain both treated and untreated patients (positivity), and it only equals the causal effect if \(L\) makes the groups exchangeable — which raises the question, which variables belong in \(L\)? Throw in too few and the bias survives; put in the wrong ones — a mediator, a collider — and you create fresh bias(see Chapter 11).
Conditional exchangeability is not magic; we can watch it work. The confounding gap above was 0.061 over the whole cohort. Compare the treated and untreated within strata of severity and most of it disappears:


Show code
cohort |>
  mutate(severity_q = cut(severity, quantile(severity, seq(0, 1, 0.2)),
                          include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(severity_q) |>
  summarise(`E[Y(0)|treated]`   = mean(risk0[drug == 1]),
            `E[Y(0)|untreated]` = mean(risk0[drug == 0]),
            gap = `E[Y(0)|treated]` - `E[Y(0)|untreated]`, .groups = "drop") |>
  kbl(digits = 3,
      caption = "Within strata of severity the untreated-risk gap nearly closes. The residue is the other measured confounders (age, diabetes).") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)




Within strata of severity the untreated-risk gap nearly closes. The residue is the other measured confounders (age, diabetes).

Inside a severity band the treated and untreated would have run nearly the same risk untreated: that is conditional exchangeability appearing in the data. The small remaining gap is the part of the confounding carried by age and diabetes, which a full adjustment set would also have to absorb — the subject of the next two chapters.
But notice what licensed that picture: we read risk0 for the treated — a counterfactual column only the oracle supplies. A real study cannot draw this table, so conditional exchangeability is never something the data confirm; it is an assumption, defended by argument about which confounders were measured and overturned by the one that was not. The disciplined response to that irreducible doubt is a sensitivity analysis — asking how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to explain the effect away. The E-value makes the question concrete: the minimum association such a confounder would need with both treatment and outcome to account for the observed effect.7 Chapter 19 takes this up in full.

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
text:
11.5 The do-operator, and the do-calculus
Potential outcomes have a twin notation, due to Pearl, that will briefly reappear when we turn to graphs. Writing \(P\!\left(Y \mid \mathrm{do}(A=a)\right)\) means the distribution of \(Y\) in the world where treatment is set to \(a\) by intervention — as opposed to \(P(Y \mid A=a)\), the distribution among those merely observed to take \(a\). The two differ when there is confounding. The bridge is an identity: \(E[Y(a)] = E\!\left[Y \mid \mathrm{do}(A=a)\right]\) — “the average potential outcome” and “the mean under intervention” are two names for one quantity. Potential outcomes and the do-operator are alternative notations, not rival theories; we use the first for stating estimands and the second when we reason on a diagram.
The do-notation leads to Pearl’s do-calculus, which is based on three rules that rewrite an expression containing \(\mathrm{do}(\cdot)\) into one without it — into ordinary conditional probabilities estimable from observational data — using only the structure of the causal graph (Chapter 11). The adjustment formula of the previous section, \(E[Y \mid \mathrm{do}(A=a)] = \sum_l E[Y \mid A=a, L=l]\,P(L=l)\), is the most familiar thing the rules deliver: the algebraic face of the backdoor criterion. When no set of measured variables blocks the back doors, the same calculus can sometimes still identify the effect by another route — the front-door formula of Chapter 18 is the classic case. The calculus is complete, if a causal effect can be identified from the assumed graph and observational data by any means. Then the three rules can derive a formula for it. And if they cannot, then the causal effect is unidentifiable in principe without extra assumptions. This book mostly uses potential outcomes and the backdoor criterion, which carry us through most applied problems. The do-calculus is the general engine behind them — invoked explicitly when sutting the back door (Chapter 18) and when we simulate interventions wholesale to form a posterior over the causal contrast (Chapter 25).
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
section: 11.6 The question, and the road from here
text:
11.6 The question, and the road from here
The framework lets us write the master-cohort question without ambiguity. Does the drug prevent stroke? becomes: estimate \(\text{ATE} = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]\) (or its risk ratio), the contrast of two counterfactual worlds. We have seen that the crude comparison estimates the wrong thing, that the error is a specific confounding term, and that three assumptions — conditional exchangeability, positivity, consistency — would license the g-formula to recover the right one. What remains is a division of labour the rest of Part III carries out:

Which variables make the groups exchangeable, and which would wreck the estimate if included — Chapter 11 (causal diagrams) answers this by reading the structure off a graph.
How to compute \(E[Y(a)]\) from those variables — Chapter 12 does it by hand, with standardisation and weighting, and Chapter 28 does it with a fitted Bayesian model and full posterior uncertainty.

The potential-outcome notation is what makes it possible by stating the target clearly.
A word of caution. This counterfactual apparatus is an operational convenience for reasoning about interventions, not a theory of physical or biological causation, and it is only as meaningful as the intervention it names. For a manipulable treatment — give the drug or not — \(Y(a)\) is crisp. For an attribute that no experiment could assign — the effect of a fixed characteristic, say — “\(Y(a)\)” can be ill defined, because there is no agreed action that sets it, and different imagined interventions yield different effects. When the intervention is vague, the estimand is vague, so that the first question of a causal analysis is not “what is the effect?”, but “the effect of which intervention, in which population?” No case presses that question harder than race.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
section: 11.7 A hard case: causal questions about race
text:
11.7 A hard case: causal questions about race
Race is the paradigm fixed attribute: there is no agreed action that sets a person’s race, so \(Y(\text{race})\) has no settled referent, and Holland’s slogan — no causation without manipulation — seems to rule the question out of court. Yet discrimination based on race is urgently in need of causal answers. The counterfactual framework’s response is to force a sharper question: intervene on what? Before taking that turn, a dissent is worth registering: a strand of epidemiology holds that the overall association of race or sex with an outcome is itself a legitimate target — a description of how much disadvantage tracks the category, and a natural starting point for disparities research, with the hunt for manipulable pathways coming second.8
Move the intervention from the person to the signal. A hiring manager does not respond to an applicant’s race in some metaphysical sense; she responds to what she perceives at the moment of decision — a name, a photograph, a voice, a postcode. Reframe the estimand as the effect of that perceived signal, assessed at the decision point — the move Greiner and Rubin formalise as the causal effect of a perceived immutable characteristic. The potential outcomes — the application that signals one race versus an otherwise identical application that signals another — are now well defined and manipulable.
The hiring case, done cleanly. This is the audit, or correspondence, study. Bertrand and Mullainathan sent employers résumés identical but for racially associated names (“Emily and Greg” versus “Lakisha and Jamal”) and measured call-backs. Because the signal is randomised over otherwise identical applications, consistency, no-interference and exchangeability hold by construction: this is a genuine randomised experiment, and the call-back gap is a clean causal estimate. Note carefully what the estimand is and is not. It is the effect of the perceived racial signal on this decision, at this stage, for the applications studied. It is not “the effect of being Black” over a life, and cannot be — but it answers a real question, squarely within the counterfactual paradigm.
Race as a bundle, not an atom. Generalising beyond a single signal, Sen and Wasow propose treating race as a bundle of sticks — a composite of manipulable constituents (name, dialect, skin tone, neighbourhood, signalled class) — and studying one stick at a time. “The effect of race” then dissolves into a family of sharper, answerable questions about components, and the analyst must say which.
Disparate treatment, disparate impact. The two notions map onto causal language. Disparate treatment — being handled differently because of race — is naturally a direct effect: the effect of the racial signal not operating through legitimate qualifications. Disparate impact — a neutral rule that falls unequally — is closer to a total effect, or a population disparity. This mapping (developed by VanderWeele and Robinson) is useful, but it is also where the trouble resides, because a direct effect asks us to hold qualifications fixed while changing race.
The open problem Kohler-Hausmann argues that the counterfactual recipe — change race, hold all else equal — misconstrues what race is. Race is not a detachable treatment applied to an otherwise-fixed person; it is constitutive of the very covariates one would hold constant — the name, the neighbourhood, the schooling, the accumulated qualifications, even how the applicant is perceived. There is then no coherent possible world in which this person is of a different race yet identical in everything race helped produce, so the “all else equal” contrast has no determinate meaning. Discrimination, on this view, is a property of a social and institutional process and of a constructed category, and calls for a constructivist account rather than a swap-and-compare counterfactual. The manipulationist reply — that the audit study still answers a well-posed question about identical applications — does not fully dissolve the objection, because “identical except the signal” is itself a stipulation that brackets all the upstream ways race shaped those résumés to begin with. (Similar critique has been made for sex, by Hu and Kohler-Hausmann.) This debate is not settled; it runs along disciplinary lines — economics and statistics largely at ease with the signal-manipulation estimand, much of law and sociology insisting it misses the structural phenomenon. The machine-learning notion of counterfactual fairness (Kusner et al.) — a decision is fair if it is unchanged in a world where the protected attribute and its descendants were different — bites the bullet by positing a full structural model with race as a root cause, and so inherits Kohler-Hausmann’s worry: it must commit to how race causes everything downstream.
Conclusion The counterfactual framework does not forbid causal questions about race; it disciplines them. It insists you name the manipulable thing — a signal, a perception, a component, or a policy — and then report the effect of that, in a population, rather than an undefined “effect of race”. Sometimes the appropriate quantity is descriptive — how much of a disparity is accounted for by measured factors (a decomposition), not a causal effect at all — and saying so plainly is part of the discipline. The one move the counterfactual framework rules out without exception is regressing the outcome on race alongside a grab-bag of controls and reading the race coefficient as “the effect of race”. That is the effect of no defined intervention, adjusted by whatever happened to enter the model — the Table-2 fallacy (Chapter 26).

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
text:
11.8 Key points

Each unit has two potential outcomes, \(Y(1)\) and \(Y(0)\); their contrast is the individual effect, and only one is ever observed (the fundamental problem).
Consistency (\(Y = Y(A)\)) and no interference tie the notation to data and require a well-defined intervention.
The targets are estimands chosen in advance — ATE, ATT, ATU — reported on a chosen scale (risk difference, risk ratio, odds ratio).
The crude contrast equals the effect plus a confounding term, \(E[Y(0)\mid A{=}1] - E[Y(0)\mid A{=}0]\).
An effect is identified under conditional exchangeability, positivity, and consistency, via standardisation / the g-formula — but the formula cannot tell you which variables to condition on (Chapter 11) or how to estimate it (Chapters 12, 24), and exchangeability itself is untestable, to be probed by sensitivity analysis (the E-value, Chapter 19).
\(E[Y(a)] = E[Y\mid \mathrm{do}(A=a)]\) links potential outcomes to Pearl’s do-operator; the do-calculus is the complete engine for deciding identifiability from a graph, used in Chapters 18 and 24.
For a fixed attribute like race, “the effect of race” is an undefined intervention, but the framework licenses sharper estimands — the effect of a perceived signal (audit studies), of a component (race as a bundle of sticks), or of a policy. Whether such reframing captures structural discrimination is a genuine open problem (Kohler-Hausmann).

title: 11  The potential-outcomes framework
text:
11.9 Exercises

Decompose the bias. Verify numerically the identity \(E[Y\mid A{=}1]-E[Y\mid A{=}0] = \text{ATT} + \{E[Y(0)\mid A{=}1]-E[Y(0)\mid A{=}0]\}\) on the cohort (use the oracle for the counterfactual term). By how much does the confounding term have to fall before the crude contrast turns protective?
Positivity, by hand. Find a stratum of severity (say, the top 1%) and check the proportion treated. What happens to the standardisation formula if some stratum has no untreated patients? Relate your answer to why extreme confounding and positivity violations travel together.
Randomise it. Modify the generator so that drug is assigned by a fair coin independent of severity. Recompute the crude contrast and the ATE. Why does marginal exchangeability now hold, and why does the confounding term vanish?
Conceptual: which intervention? A colleague wants “the causal effect of obesity on stroke”. Using consistency and the well-defined-intervention idea, explain why this estimand is ambiguous, and rewrite it as a question with a manipulable treatment.
do and see. In your own words, give an example of two quantities \(P(Y\mid A=a)\) and \(P(Y\mid \mathrm{do}(A=a))\) that are equal, and two that are not, and say what feature of the cohort makes the difference.
Make the question answerable. A team wants “the causal effect of race on hiring.”

Reframe it as the effect of a manipulable signal and sketch an audit study that would estimate it, stating precisely what the estimand does and does not cover.
Explain Kohler-Hausmann’s objection that “change race, hold qualifications fixed” is incoherent, and argue whether your audit estimand escapes it.

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.1 A graph of causal assumptions
A DAG has three ingredients and no more.
A path is any route between two nodes along the edges, ignoring their direction. A directed path follows the arrows head-to-tail. \(B\) is a descendant of \(A\) if a directed path runs from \(A\) to \(B\).
The single most important thing about a DAG is what it does not contain. Drawing \(A \rightarrow B\) is a weak claim: there might be an effect. Omitting the arrow is a strong one: there is no direct effect, in any individual, of any size. A DAG is therefore a compact statement of causal assumptions, brought to the data from subject knowledge — physiology, study design, common sense — and not learned from the data themselves. The data can occasionally embarrass a DAG (see the fine print at the end), but they can never hand you one.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
Nodes are variables — severity, drug, stroke.
A directed edge \(A \rightarrow B\) says \(A\) may exert a direct causal effect on \(B\): intervene on \(A\), holding the rest of the graph’s logic fixed, and \(B\) can change. “Direct” means not routed through another node already drawn.
Acyclic means you cannot follow the arrows and return to where you started. Nothing is its own ancestor; causes precede effects.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.2 The three elementary structures
Every path, however long, is assembled from three elementary three-node pieces. Learn how each one transmits or stops association and you can read any graph.


Show code
co <- list(x = c(X = 0, Z = 1, Y = 2), y = c(X = 0, Z = 0, Y = 0))
chain <- dagify(Z ~ X, Y ~ Z, coords = co)
fork  <- dagify(X ~ Z, Y ~ Z, coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Z = 1, Y = 2),
                                             y = c(X = 0, Z = 1, Y = 0)))
coll  <- dagify(Z ~ X, Z ~ Y, coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Z = 1, Y = 2),
                                             y = c(X = 0, Z = -1, Y = 0)))
mk <- function(d, ttl) ggdag(d, node_size = 16, text_size = 3.2, edge_type = "link") +
  theme_dag() + ggtitle(ttl) + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5))
mk(chain, "Chain:  X -> Z -> Y") |
  mk(fork, "Fork:  X <- Z -> Y") |
  mk(coll, "Collider:  X -> Z <- Y")





The three elementary structures. A chain and a fork both transmit association along the path; a collider does not. The grey node is the one a path runs through.





A chain, \(X \rightarrow Z \rightarrow Y\), is mediation. \(Z\) is a mediator: the effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) runs through it. \(X\) and \(Y\) are associated; condition on \(Z\) and the association is blocked, because once you fix the middle of the relay there is nothing left for \(X\) to tell you about \(Y\).
A fork, \(X \leftarrow Z \rightarrow Y\), is confounding. \(Z\) is a common cause. \(X\) and \(Y\) are associated even though neither causes the other — a purely spurious correlation. Condition on \(Z\) and it blocks: within a level of \(Z\) the spurious channel is shut.
A collider, \(X \rightarrow Z \leftarrow Y\), is the mirror image and the one that trips people. \(Z\) is a common effect. Here \(X\) and \(Y\) are not associated through \(Z\) — the path is blocked by default. Conditioning on \(Z\) does the opposite of what it does in the other two structures: it opens the path and manufactures an association out of nothing.

The collider’s reversal is worth a sentence of intuition. If \(Z\) is high and depends on both \(X\) and \(Y\), then learning \(X\) was low tells you \(Y\) was probably high — because something had to push \(Z\) up. Two independent causes of a shared effect become dependent once you hold the effect fixed. We will see this is the engine of selection bias.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.3 What adjustment does: three simulations
The claims above are not stylistic preferences; they are arithmetic, and on data whose truth we control we can watch each one happen. In every panel below “adjustment” is just adding the middle node to a linear regression of \(Y\) on \(X\), and there is no direct \(X \rightarrow Y\) effect anywhere — every \(X\)–\(Y\) association we see is structural.

n <- 5000
## FORK:  X <- Z -> Y   (Z is a confounder; no X -> Y)
Z <- rnorm(n); X <- 0.9 * Z + rnorm(n); Y <- 0.9 * Z + rnorm(n)
fork_crude <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))["X"]          # spurious association
fork_adj   <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))["X"]      # adjust the confounder
c(crude = fork_crude, adjusted_for_Z = fork_adj)

         crude.X adjusted_for_Z.X 
      0.41929838      -0.00800076 


In the fork, the crude slope is a clear 0.42 — a confound posing as an effect — and conditioning on \(Z\) collapses it to -0.01. This is the case the reflex gets right: adjust for the common cause.

## CHAIN:  X -> M -> Y   (M is a mediator; no direct X -> Y)
X <- rnorm(n); M <- 0.9 * X + rnorm(n); Y <- 0.9 * M + rnorm(n)
chain_total <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))["X"]         # the total effect of X
chain_adj   <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + M))["X"]     # adjust the mediator
c(total = chain_total, adjusted_for_M = chain_adj)

         total.X adjusted_for_M.X 
     0.816156525      0.005980602 


In the chain, the crude slope 0.82 is the effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) — the thing we want. Conditioning on the mediator \(M\) destroys it, leaving 0.01. Here the reflex is wrong: control for \(M\) and you have adjusted away the very effect you set out to measure. The same drug, the same data, the wrong number.

## COLLIDER:  X -> C <- Y   (C is a common effect; X and Y are independent)
X <- rnorm(n); Y <- rnorm(n); C <- 0.9 * X + 0.9 * Y + rnorm(n)
coll_crude <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))["X"]          # truly independent
coll_adj   <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + C))["X"]      # condition on the collider
c(crude = coll_crude, adjusted_for_C = coll_adj)

         crude.X adjusted_for_C.X 
     -0.01024442      -0.45277671 


In the collider, \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent by construction, and the crude slope duly sits at -0.01. Condition on \(C\) and a association of -0.45 appears from nowhere. Adjusting created the bias. No amount of data fixes this; more rows estimate the spurious slope more precisely.
Three structures, three different right answers, one wrong reflex. “Control for everything you can measure” silently treats every variable as a fork. It is correct for confounders, ruinous for mediators, and actively bias-inducing for colliders. The graph is what tells them apart.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.4 One rule underneath: d-separation
The three cases are special instances of a single criterion. Take any path between \(X\) and \(Y\), and a set of variables \(Z\) you have conditioned on. The path is blocked if either:

it contains a non-collider (a chain link or a fork centre) that is in \(Z\); or
it contains a collider that is not in \(Z\) — and none of that collider’s descendants is in \(Z\) either.

If every path between \(X\) and \(Y\) is blocked, they are d-separated given \(Z\), and the graph guarantees they are statistically independent given \(Z\). If even one path is open, they are d-connected and we expect an association.
Two corollaries are the whole game. Conditioning on a non-collider (rule 1) helps — it shuts a path. Conditioning on a collider, or on anything downstream of one (rule 2), hurts — it opens a path that was closed. That parenthetical about descendants is the subtle part: you need not put the collider itself in \(Z\) to do the damage; a proxy for it — a variable it causes — is enough. Selection into a sample is exactly such a proxy.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.5 The backdoor criterion
Now the payoff. We want the causal effect of an exposure \(A\) on an outcome \(Y\). The paths from \(A\) to \(Y\) come in two kinds:

Causal (directed) paths, \(A \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow Y\), which start with an arrow out of \(A\). These carry the effect; we must leave them open.
Backdoor paths, which start with an arrow into \(A\) (e.g. \(A \leftarrow Z \rightarrow Y\)). These carry confounding; we must close them all.

A set \(Z\) satisfies the backdoor criterion for the effect of \(A\) on \(Y\) when

no node in \(Z\) is a descendant of \(A\) (so we touch neither mediators nor colliders on the causal side), and
\(Z\) blocks every backdoor path from \(A\) to \(Y\).

When such a \(Z\) exists, conditioning on it makes the treated and untreated exchangeable within levels of \(Z\) — exactly the conditional exchangeability of Chapter 10 — and the effect is identified: we may estimate it by standardising or weighting over \(Z\) (Chapter 12). The three structures reappear as a vocabulary: an open backdoor path is confounding; a directed path is mediation (block it and you lose part of the effect); a path opened by conditioning on a common effect is selection bias.
Crucially, the criterion can forbid adjustment. A mediator is a descendant of \(A\), so rule 1 keeps it out of \(Z\) for the total effect. A collider, if not conditioned on, already blocks its path, so adding it can only do harm. The graph turns “what should I adjust for?” from a matter of taste into a matter of reading.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
section: 12.6 The master cohort, as a graph
text:
12.6 The master cohort, as a graph
Our running cohort — does a blood-pressure drug prevent stroke? — is built from a known data-generating process (R/simulate_cohort.R). Every structural equation is one or more arrows, and together they make the DAG below.

mc <- dagify(
  diabetes     ~ age,
  severity     ~ age + diabetes,
  drug         ~ severity + diabetes + pref,        # confounding-by-indication + instrument
  sbp          ~ age + severity + drug,             # the drug lowers blood pressure
  stroke       ~ severity + age + diabetes + sbp + drug,
  hospitalised ~ drug + stroke,                     # a common effect
  exposure = "drug", outcome = "stroke",
  coords = list(
    x = c(age = 0, diabetes = 0, severity = 1.1, pref = 1.5, drug = 2.5, sbp = 3.6,
          stroke = 4.8, hospitalised = 3.6),
    y = c(age = 2.6, diabetes = 0.6, severity = 1.6, pref = 3.5, drug = 2.5, sbp = 3.4,
          stroke = 1.7, hospitalised = -0.2)))



Show code
ggdag_status(mc, text = FALSE, use_labels = "name",
             node_size = 9, text_size = 3.2, edge_type = "link") +
  theme_dag() +
  guides(color = "none", fill = "none") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  expand_limits(x = c(-0.4, 5.4), y = c(-0.6, 3.9))





The master-cohort DAG. drug (exposure) and stroke (outcome) in blue; severity and diabetes are common causes (confounders); sbp is a mediator on the causal path drug -> sbp -> stroke; pref is an instrument; hospitalised is a collider (a common effect of drug and stroke).




Reading it off: severity and diabetes sit on forks into both drug and stroke — they are the confounders. sbp is the mediator, lying on the causal path drug → sbp → stroke (the drug works largely by lowering blood pressure). pref, the prescribing preference, points only into drug: it is an instrument (Chapter 17), not a confounder. And hospitalised is a collider — a common effect of treatment and stroke — sitting off to the side.
We need not eyeball which adjustments are valid; the graph computes them.

adjustmentSets(mc, exposure = "drug", outcome = "stroke", effect = "total")

{ diabetes, severity }


dagitty returns { diabetes, severity }: blocking the two forks suffices for the total effect, and age and pref are optional (adjusting age is harmless; adjusting the instrument pref is allowed but pointless and, in general, can hurt precision). Notice what is absent: sbp is never in an adjustment set for the total effect, because it is a mediator; hospitalised never appears, because it is a collider.
The cohort was engineered so the crude analysis reverses the truth. The graph predicts exactly that — there is a wide-open backdoor drug ← severity → stroke — and predicts the cure.

df <- simulate_cohort(n = 10000, seed = 2024)
df$age_c <- (df$age - 62) / 10
truth <- cohort_truth(df)

crude_RR <- with(df, mean(stroke[drug == 1]) / mean(stroke[drug == 0]))

g_RR <- function(rhs) {                          # standardise (a peek at Ch. 12)
  m  <- glm(as.formula(paste("stroke ~", rhs)), binomial, df)
  r1 <- mean(predict(m, transform(df, drug = 1), type = "response"))
  r0 <- mean(predict(m, transform(df, drug = 0), type = "response"))
  r1 / r0
}
c(crude             = crude_RR,
  backdoor_set      = g_RR("drug + severity + age_c + diabetes"),
  plus_mediator_sbp = g_RR("drug + severity + age_c + diabetes + sbp"),
  TRUTH             = truth$ATE_RR)

            crude      backdoor_set plus_mediator_sbp             TRUTH 
        1.5665432         0.6103411         0.7216460         0.6012111 


The crude risk ratio is 1.57 — the drug looks harmful. Adjust the backdoor set the graph prescribed and it flips to 0.61, essentially the true 0.6: protective. Now obey the reflex and “adjust for blood pressure too”: the estimate drifts back to 0.72, because sbp is a mediator and conditioning on it blocks the very pathway the drug acts through. The graph said all of this in advance. (The estimation machinery — standardisation — is Chapter 12’s subject; here it is only a witness.)
What if we wanted the drug’s direct effect, the part not mediated by blood pressure? The reflex — “add the mediator” — is again not the whole story:

adjustmentSets(mc, exposure = "drug", outcome = "stroke", effect = "direct")

{ age, diabetes, sbp, severity }


To block the mediated path we must condition on sbp — but doing so opens the collider drug → sbp ← age → stroke (blood pressure is a common effect of the drug and of age), which must then be re-closed by adding age. The valid set is { age, diabetes, severity, sbp }, not sbp alone. Direct effects are graphically treacherous in exactly this way; Chapter 15 takes up mediation properly.

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.7 Selection bias is collider bias
The collider sat quietly to one side above. It earns a section because conditioning on a collider is not an exotic mistake — it is what sampling does. When a study includes only hospitalised patients, only volunteers, only survivors, or only the non-lost-to-follow-up, it has conditioned on a variable that those things depend on. If that variable is a common effect of the exposure and the outcome (or of their causes), the selection opens a backdoor path and biases the estimate, even with no confounding at all. Hernán, Hernández-Díaz and Robins (2004) showed that the textbook menagerie of “selection biases” — Berkson’s bias, informative censoring, inappropriate control selection — is one structure wearing many hats: conditioning on a common effect.
Our hospitalised node is the canonical case. Both the drug (drug → hospitalised) and a stroke (stroke → hospitalised) raise the chance of admission. Restrict the analysis to inpatients and watch:

RR_in_hospital <- with(subset(df, hospitalised == 1),
                       mean(stroke[drug == 1]) / mean(stroke[drug == 0]))
c(among_hospitalised = RR_in_hospital, true_ATE_RR = truth$ATE_RR)

among_hospitalised        true_ATE_RR 
         0.8542160          0.6012111 


Among the hospitalised the crude risk ratio is 0.85 — pulled away from the truth purely by the act of selection, with no confounder touched. (Within a ward, treated patients are over-represented among the not-very-sick admissions, so the treated and untreated are no longer comparable.)
The pattern recurs across epidemiology, and it really does reverse conclusions:

Berkson’s bias. Two independent diseases appear correlated in a hospital sample, because having either raises the chance of admission — the admission is the collider.
The “birth-weight paradox”. Among low-birth-weight infants, maternal smoking appears protective against infant mortality. Hernández-Díaz, Schisterman and Hernán (2006) used a DAG to show this is collider bias: birth weight is a common effect of smoking and of unmeasured causes of mortality, so stratifying on it manufactures the inverse association. The drug-sbp collider we just met for the direct effect is the same structure.
COVID-19 risk factors. Griffith and colleagues (2020) showed that analysing only people tested for SARS-CoV-2 (a sample selected on health-care contact, symptoms and behaviour) induces collider associations strong enough to distort estimated risk factors for infection and severity.

This is also the formal resolution of the intuition-trap flagged back in Chapter 3: the mind, which is good at imagining how two things might share a cause, is bad at noticing when it has accidentally selected on a shared effect.

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.8 The fine print
A DAG is a powerful instrument with sharp edges, and honesty about its limits is part of using it.

It encodes assumptions, not findings. The arrows come from substantive knowledge. A wrong graph gives confident, wrong advice. Two analysts with different DAGs can both adjust “correctly” and disagree — the disagreement is about the science, which is where it belongs, now made explicit.
It is mostly untestable — but not entirely. A DAG implies a list of conditional independencies that the data can contradict. Our graph implies, for instance, that the instrument is independent of the confounder, pref ⊥ severity:


round(cor(df$pref, df$severity), 3)     # the DAG implies ~ 0

[1] -0.005


The observed correlation is -0.005. A gross violation would falsify the graph; agreement is reassuring but never proves it, since many different DAGs can share the same independencies. - It is nonparametric. A DAG says whether a path transmits association, never how much. It cannot tell you the magnitude or even the direction of a bias — only that one is present. Quantifying “how bad could an unmeasured confounder be?” is the job of sensitivity analysis (Chapter 19), which leans on the fact that our severity is only partly measured. - It assumes the standard background conditions — the causal Markov condition (a variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents), no hidden cycles, and a coherent time order. Feedback over time, where sbp is a confounder of later treatment and a mediator of earlier treatment, breaks the single static picture and needs the time-indexed graphs of Chapter 14.
What the DAG buys, in return, is the thing Chapter 10 could not give: a procedure, checkable by anyone, for turning a causal story into a list of variables to adjust for — and a list to leave alone.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
section: 12.9 What a DAG cannot show: interaction and mechanism
text:
12.9 What a DAG cannot show: interaction and mechanism
Even a correct DAG, used for a question it answers well, is silent about the thing students most often want to read off it: how causes combine. An arrow records that a cause acts; it says nothing about the shape of that action. This deserves more than the one-line “it is nonparametric” of the fine print, because it is the limit most often forgotten in practice.
Take the simplest case — an exposure A and a second cause V of the outcome Y, both randomised so there is no confounding at all. The DAG is A → Y ← V, full stop. Now build two different worlds on that one diagram: in the first, A lowers risk by the same amount whatever V; in the second, A helps only when V = 0.

set.seed(11); n <- 40000
V <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5); A <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)          # A -> Y <- V, with A independent of V
base    <- 0.30 + 0.20 * V                              # outcome risk with no treatment
Y_const <- rbinom(n, 1, base - 0.10 * A)                # A helps everyone equally
Y_modif <- rbinom(n, 1, base - 0.20 * A * (V == 0))     # A helps only when V = 0
rd <- function(Y, v) mean(Y[A == 1 & V == v]) - mean(Y[A == 0 & V == v])
c(const_V0 = rd(Y_const, 0), const_V1 = rd(Y_const, 1),
  modif_V0 = rd(Y_modif, 0), modif_V1 = rd(Y_modif, 1))

   const_V0    const_V1    modif_V0    modif_V1 
-0.09116449 -0.10143784 -0.19510318 -0.00381562 


Both columns of data come from the same graph and license the same adjustment set (here, none). Yet in the first world the risk difference is about -0.09 whether or not V is present; in the second it is -0.2 when V = 0 and essentially 0 when V = 1. The drug is worth giving to everyone, or only to half the patients — and the DAG cannot tell you which, because effect modification lives in the functional form of the structural equation, not in the topology of the arrows.
This is a limitation and a feature at once.

As a limitation, you cannot read effect modification, dose–response, thresholds, or synergy off a DAG. Two analysts who agree on every arrow may still disagree about whether the effect is uniform, and they must settle it with a model — an interaction term, a stratified estimate — not with the picture. Worse, whether interaction is even present can flip with the scale you measure it on (additive versus multiplicative), and the graph is mute on scale entirely. That is the whole subject of Chapter 16, where the master cohort’s diabetes is engineered so additive interaction is present while the multiplicative interaction vanishes — a distinction no DAG could record.
As a feature, because the graph commits to no functional form, its verdicts about confounding and adjustment are robust to whatever that form turns out to be. d-separation holds no matter how A and V combine to make Y. The DAG answers “which variables?” precisely because it refuses to answer “how much, and in what shape?”

A few specialised diagrams reach past these limits when you need them. Single-world intervention graphs (SWIGs) splice the intervention into the graph to make counterfactual independencies explicit; sufficient-component-cause diagrams (the “causal pies” of Chapter 16) represent mechanistic interaction — two factors co-participating in one sufficient cause — a different idea from statistical interaction that a DAG was never built to carry. The working rule: use the DAG to decide what to condition on, and a model (Chapters 16, 20–21) to describe how the effect behaves once you have.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.10 Drawing a DAG: a step-by-step
A DAG is only as good as the thinking behind it, and that thinking has a workable routine. The order matters: most mistakes come from drawing arrows before fixing the question and the time line.

State the question first. Name the exposure A, the outcome Y, the estimand (total effect? direct effect? — they need different graphs and different adjustment sets, as we saw above), the target population, and time zero. A DAG is built for a question; you cannot draw one in the abstract.
List the variables, generously. Write down A, Y, and every plausible common cause of them you can think of — measured and unmeasured. Do not filter yet: a variable left off the page is a stronger assumption than one drawn on it.
Put them in time order. Lay the nodes out left to right by when each is determined; arrows may only point forward in time. This one discipline prevents cycles and exposes the commonest blunder — treating a post-exposure variable as a baseline confounder.
Draw the direct effects. For each ordered pair ask: would intervening on the earlier variable change the later one, by a route not already drawn through another node? If yes, draw the arrow. “Direct” is always relative to the variables on the page.
Add unmeasured common causes explicitly. If two nodes share a cause you did not measure, draw it as a latent node U. This is where most confounding hides, and an honest U is worth more than a tidy graph that pretends it away.
Be conservative with arrows, not with nodes. When unsure whether a confounding arrow belongs, include it — omission is the strong claim. But do not invent implausible arrows just to look safe; every arrow is a claim you must be able to defend.
Read the missing arrows back. For each absent edge, say it aloud: “I am asserting no direct effect here, in any patient, of any size — am I comfortable with that?” If not, add it. Then confirm the graph is acyclic.
Label the roles. Mark A and Y, and classify every other node — confounder (fork), mediator (on a causal path), collider (common effect), instrument, competing exposure. The role dictates the treatment, not the variable’s name or how “important” it feels.
Find the adjustment set, then sanity-check it. Derive it by hand (block every backdoor path; touch no descendant of A) or with software, then ask whether positivity is plausible for it: are there treated and untreated patients at every combination of its values (Chapter 10)?
Test what is testable. The graph implies conditional independencies; check a few against the data. A gross violation means the graph — not the data — is wrong.
Show it, and draw the rivals. Hand the DAG to a colleague who knows the substance, then draw the alternative DAGs you cannot rule out and see whether the adjustment set survives them. Where it does not, that is the target for sensitivity analysis (Chapter 19).

The dagitty/ggdag workflow makes steps 7–10 mechanical:

library(dagitty); library(ggdag)
g <- dagify(Y ~ A + L + U,            # the outcome's direct causes
            A ~ L + U,                # the exposure's direct causes (L measured, U not)
            exposure = "A", outcome = "Y",
            latent   = "U")           # mark the unmeasured node
ggdag(g)                              # step 7: eyeball the structure
adjustmentSets(g)                     # step 9: a valid set, if one exists
impliedConditionalIndependencies(g)   # step 10: what the data can falsify

If adjustmentSets() comes back empty, no measured set identifies the effect — the honest signal to reach for an instrument (Chapter 17), a quasi-experiment (Chapter 18), or a sensitivity analysis (Chapter 19), rather than to keep piling on covariates.
Five mistakes the routine is built to prevent.

Adjusting for a mediator — or any descendant of the exposure — which blocks part of the very effect you want (the drug → sbp lesson, and the “Table 2 fallacy” of Chapter 26).
Conditioning on a collider, most insidiously through sample selection.
Reversed or muddled time order, which lets a consequence masquerade as a cause.
Forgetting unmeasured common causes — the tidy-graph trap of step 5.
Choosing variables by what moves the estimate — a stepwise habit that will happily add colliders and drop confounders, because “it changed the coefficient” is not evidence that adjustment was warranted.
crumbs: Part III. Formal causation: counterfactuals and graphs

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
section: 12.11 Structural equations: the model behind the graph
text:
12.11 Structural equations: the model behind the graph
A DAG, we keep saying, throws away the functional form and keeps only the arrows. It is worth seeing exactly what it throws away, because that fuller object — a structural causal model (SCM) — is something this book has been using all along.
An SCM writes one equation per variable, expressing it as a function of its direct causes (its parents on the graph) and an independent disturbance \(U\): \[ V_i \;=\; f_i(\text{parents}_i,\; U_i). \] The arrows of the DAG are read straight off these equations: draw an edge from every argument of \(f_i\) into \(V_i\). The graph is the skeleton of the SCM — what is left when you forget each \(f_i\) and the distribution of each \(U_i\): \[ \text{SCM} \;=\; \text{DAG} \;+\; \text{functional forms} \;+\; \text{noise distributions}. \] This is precisely why the interaction limitation above holds — modification, dose–response and scale all live inside the \(f_i\), which the DAG has discarded.
The master cohort makes it concrete, because R/simulate_cohort.R is an SCM: a system of structural equations, read top to bottom in causal order. A few of them, schematically:
severity = 0.40·age_c + 0.50·diabetes + U_sev          →  age, diabetes  →  severity
drug     ~ Bernoulli(logit⁻¹(−0.6 + 1.4·severity
                     + 0.3·diabetes + 1.3·pref))        →  severity, diabetes, pref  →  drug
sbp      = 145 + 7·severity + 1.5·age_c − 12·drug + U_sbp  →  severity, age, drug  →  sbp
stroke   ~ Bernoulli(exp(… + 0.20·sbp − 0.25·drug + …))    →  severity, age, diabetes, sbp, drug  →  stroke
The DAG drawn earlier in this chapter is exactly the skeleton of this code: every coefficient is an arrow, every rnorm/rbinom an independent \(U\). We have been reasoning about the shadow of a model whose every detail we happen to know — which is what lets it serve as an answer key.
Intervention is surgery on the equations. To ask “what if everyone took the drug?”, the SCM does not nudge a coefficient; it deletes the equation for drug and replaces it with the constant 1, leaving every other equation untouched. On the graph this is graph surgery — erase the arrows into drug, keep the arrows out — and it is Pearl’s \(do(\text{drug}=1)\) operator. It is identical to the potential outcome \(Y(1)\) of Chapter 10, and it is exactly how the cohort’s oracle was built: evaluate the outcome equation under drug = 1 and again under drug = 0, on the same draws of the noise.

truth$ATE_RD     # E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]: the outcome equation under do(drug=1) vs do(drug=0)

[1] -0.02682689


The backdoor criterion is, underneath, a claim about this surgery: a set blocks the backdoor paths exactly when adjusting for it makes the observed association equal to the association in the mutilated graph — the world in which the arrows into drug have been cut.
Where classical SEM fits. The structural-equation models of the path-analysis tradition — linear equations, standardised “path coefficients”, often with latent factors — are the linear-Gaussian special case of an SCM: assume every \(f_i\) is linear and every \(U_i\) Gaussian, and d-separation collapses to Wright’s old rules for tracing paths. The modern advance was not the equations, which are a century old, but the separation of concerns: the DAG carries the causal assumptions (qualitative, arguable from knowledge) while the equations carry the estimation assumptions (functional form, distributions). Classical SEM tended to fuse the two, and so could not say which of its conclusions rested on causal belief and which on convenient linearity.






Wright’s path-tracing rules



Sewall Wright invented path analysis in the 1920s — the direct ancestor of structural equation modelling, and decades ahead of formal DAGs. In a standardised linear model (every variable scaled to unit variance), Wright showed that the correlation between two variables is the sum, over every open path joining them, of the product of the path coefficients along that path.
A path counts as open (traceable) when

it never passes through a collider — a variable entered by two arrowheads, \(\rightarrow \bullet \leftarrow\);
it changes direction at most once, and only at a common cause (you may trace backwards against the arrows and then forwards, never forwards and then backwards); and
no variable appears on it twice.

So for a fork \(X \leftarrow Z \rightarrow Y\) with coefficients \(a\) and \(b\), the implied correlation is \(r_{XY} = ab\); for a chain \(X \rightarrow Z \rightarrow Y\) it is likewise \(ab\); for a collider \(X \rightarrow Z \leftarrow Y\) there is no open path, so \(r_{XY} = 0\). Add a direct edge \(X \rightarrow Y\) with coefficient \(c\) to the fork and the two open paths simply add: \(r_{XY} = c + ab\).
These are the three elementary structures of this chapter, and “open path” is exactly an unconditioned path with no collider. Wright’s rules are therefore the linear, unconditioned special case of d-separation: because his model was linear he could keep the magnitudes — the products and sums of coefficients — whereas d-separation discards the magnitudes and keeps only the qualitative open-or-blocked verdict. That is precisely what lets d-separation survive when the functions are nonlinear and the question is “adjust or not?” rather than “what is the correlation?”.


That separation is the division of labour the rest of the book runs on:

The DAG settles identification — can the effect be recovered from the data at hand, and what must be adjusted? This needs only qualitative knowledge and is robust to the functional form.
A fitted structural model settles estimation — what is the number, with what uncertainty? This is regression read as a counterfactual machine (Chapters 20–22) and, in full, Bayesian g-computation (Chapter 28), where the outcome equation is fit and then operated on — do(drug = 1) versus do(drug = 0) — to read off the contrast.

The two are not interchangeable, and the order is not negotiable. A richer functional form cannot rescue a wrong DAG: if the graph omits a confounding arrow, no regression, however flexible, recovers the effect. Identification first, estimation second — the graph tells you whether there is a number worth estimating; the equations tell you what it is.

title: 12  Causal diagrams (DAGs)
text:
12.12 Key points

A DAG is a statement of causal assumptions: nodes are variables, an arrow is a possible direct effect, and a missing arrow is the strong claim of no direct effect.
Every path is built from three structures. A chain (mediator) and a fork (confounder) transmit association and are blocked by conditioning; a collider (common effect) blocks by default and is opened by conditioning on it or its descendants.
“Control for everything” is wrong. It is right only for confounders; it adjusts away effects when applied to mediators and manufactures bias when applied to colliders.
d-separation is the single rule that decides independence; the backdoor criterion applies it to pick a valid adjustment set — block every backdoor path, touch no descendant of the exposure.
A valid backdoor set delivers the conditional exchangeability of Chapter 10, so the effect can be standardised or weighted (Chapter 12). For the master cohort the total-effect set is { severity, diabetes }; sbp (mediator) and hospitalised (collider) must be excluded.
Selection bias is collider bias: sampling on a common effect of exposure and outcome opens a path and biases the estimate with no confounding present.
A DAG is nonparametric: it shows whether causes act, never how they combine. Effect modification and interaction are invisible on it, and the very presence of interaction can depend on scale (Chapter 16). Use the graph to choose what to adjust for; use a model to describe how the effect behaves.
A DAG is the skeleton of a structural causal model — one equation per variable, \(V = f(\text{parents}, U)\), with the functions and noise forgotten. The DAG identifies the effect (what to adjust); the fitted equations estimate it (Chapters 20–22, 25). Intervention is surgery on the equations (\(do(\cdot)\)), and a wrong graph cannot be fixed by better equations.
